[Hungarian raids in the 9–10th centuries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_invasions_of_Europe "Hungarian invasions of Europe"): Between 899 and 970, the researchers count 47 (38 to West and 9 to East)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-Szabados_Augsburg_2005-45) raids in different parts of Europe. From these campaigns only 8 were unsuccessful and the others ended with success.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-FOOTNOTENagy2007168-46)

The foundation of the [Hungarian state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principality_of_Hungary "Principality of Hungary") is connected to the [Hungarian conquerors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_conquest_of_the_Carpathian_Basin "Hungarian conquest of the Carpathian Basin"), who arrived from the [Pontic-Caspian steppe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontic%E2%80%93Caspian_steppe "Pontic–Caspian steppe") as a confederation of [seven tribes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_chieftains_of_the_Magyars "Seven chieftains of the Magyars").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-c194-47) The [Hungarians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarians "Hungarians") arrived in the [Carpathian Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pannonian_Basin "Pannonian Basin") as a branch of a strong centralised steppe-empire under the leadership of Grand Prince [Álmos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%81lmos "Álmos") and his son [Árpád](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%81rp%C3%A1d "Árpád"): founders of the [Árpád dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%81rp%C3%A1d_dynasty "Árpád dynasty"), the Hungarian ruling dynasty and the Hungarian state. The Árpád dynasty claimed to be a direct descendant of [Attila the Hun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attila "Attila").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-:02-48)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-49)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-50) The Hungarians took possession of the area in a pre-planned manner, with a long move-in between 862 and 895.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-:2822-51) The rising Hungary conducted successful [fierce campaigns and raids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_invasions_of_Europe "Hungarian invasions of Europe"), from [Constantinople](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantinople "Constantinople") to as far as today's Spain.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-Stephen_Wyley-52) The Hungarians defeated three major East Frankish imperial armies between 907 and 910.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-53) A defeat at the [Battle of Lechfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lechfeld "Battle of Lechfeld") in 955 signalled a provisory end to most campaigns on foreign territories, at least towards the west.

#### Age of Árpádian kings

Main articles: [Kingdom of Hungary (1000–1301)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hungary_(1000%E2%80%931301) "Kingdom of Hungary (1000–1301)") and [Árpád dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%81rp%C3%A1d_dynasty "Árpád dynasty")

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/A_Szent_Korona_el%C3%B6lr%C5%91l_2.jpg/250px-A_Szent_Korona_el%C3%B6lr%C5%91l_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:A_Szent_Korona_el%C3%B6lr%C5%91l_2.jpg)

The [Holy Crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Crown_of_Hungary "Holy Crown of Hungary") (_Szent Korona_), one of the key symbols of Hungary. It was gifted to [Saint Stephen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_I_of_Hungary "Stephen I of Hungary"), the first [King of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_Hungary "King of Hungary"), who converted the nation to Christianity.

In 972, the ruling prince ([Hungarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_language "Hungarian language"): _fejedelem_) [Géza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%A9za,_Grand_Prince_of_the_Hungarians "Géza, Grand Prince of the Hungarians") of the [Árpád dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%81rp%C3%A1d_dynasty "Árpád dynasty") officially started to integrate Hungary into Christian Western Europe.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-54) His son [Saint Stephen I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_I_of_Hungary "Stephen I of Hungary") became the first [King of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_Hungary "King of Hungary") after defeating his [pagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paganism "Paganism") uncle [Koppány](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kopp%C3%A1ny "Koppány"). Under Stephen, Hungary was recognised as a Catholic [Apostolic Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apostolic_Majesty "Apostolic Majesty").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-55) Applying to [Pope Sylvester II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Sylvester_II "Pope Sylvester II"), Stephen received the insignia of royalty (including probably a part of the [Holy Crown of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Crown_of_Hungary "Holy Crown of Hungary")) from the papacy.

By 1006, Stephen consolidated his power and started sweeping reforms to convert Hungary into a Western-style [feudal state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudalism "Feudalism"). The country switched to using Latin for administration purposes, and until as late as 1844, Latin remained the official language of administration. King [Saint Ladislaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ladislaus_I_of_Hungary "Ladislaus I of Hungary") completed the work of King [Saint Stephen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_I_of_Hungary "Stephen I of Hungary"), consolidating the Hungarian state's power and strengthening [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity"). His charismatic personality, strategic leadership, and military talents resulted in the termination of internal power struggles and foreign military threats.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-Saint_Ladislaus_DNA-56) The wife of the Croatian king [Demetrius Zvonimir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demetrius_Zvonimir_of_Croatia "Demetrius Zvonimir of Croatia") was Ladislaus's sister.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-57) At [Helen's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_of_Hungary,_Queen_of_Croatia "Helen of Hungary, Queen of Croatia") request, Ladislaus intervened in the conflict and invaded Croatia in 1091.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFine1991282,_284-58) The [Kingdom of Croatia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Croatia_(925%E2%80%931102) "Kingdom of Croatia (925–1102)") entered a [personal union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Croatia_in_personal_union_with_Hungary "Croatia in personal union with Hungary") with the [Kingdom of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hungary_(1000%E2%80%931301) "Kingdom of Hungary (1000–1301)") in 1102 with the coronation of King [Coloman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloman,_King_of_Hungary "Coloman, King of Hungary") as "King of Croatia and Dalmatia" in 1102 in [Biograd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biograd_na_Moru "Biograd na Moru").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-HR-HU-Heka-59)

[![Image 18: 1097, Europe, map](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/Europe_mediterranean_1097.jpg/250px-Europe_mediterranean_1097.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Europe_mediterranean_1097.jpg)

Europe in 1097

One of the most powerful and wealthiest kings of the Árpád dynasty was [Béla III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9la_III_of_Hungary "Béla III of Hungary"),[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-60) who disposed of the equivalent of 23 tonnes of silver per year, according to a contemporary [income register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Income_register_of_B%C3%A9la_III_of_Hungary "Income register of Béla III of Hungary"). This exceeded the income of the French king (estimated at 17 tonnes) and was double the receipts of the English Crown.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-61)[Andrew II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_II_of_Hungary "Andrew II of Hungary") issued the _[Diploma Andreanum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diploma\_Andreanum "Diploma Andreanum")_ which secured the special privileges of the [Transylvanian Saxons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transylvanian_Saxons "Transylvanian Saxons") and is considered the first [autonomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous_administrative_division "Autonomous administrative division") law in the world.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-62) He led the [Fifth Crusade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_Crusade "Fifth Crusade") to the [Holy Land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Land "Holy Land") in 1217, setting up the largest royal army in the history of Crusades. His [Golden Bull of 1222](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Bull_of_1222 "Golden Bull of 1222") was the first constitution in [Continental Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Europe "Continental Europe"). The lesser nobles also began to present Andrew with grievances, a practice that evolved into the institution of the parliament (_parlamentum publicum_).

In 1241–1242, the kingdom received a major blow with the [Mongol (Tatar) invasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongolian_invasion_of_Hungary "Mongolian invasion of Hungary"). Up to half of Hungary's population of 2 million were victims of the invasion.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-63) King [Béla IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9la_IV_of_Hungary "Béla IV of Hungary") let [Cumans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumans "Cumans") and [Jassic people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jasz_people "Jasz people"), who were fleeing the Mongols, into the country.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-64) Over the centuries, they were fully assimilated.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-65) After the Mongols retreated, King Béla ordered the construction of hundreds of stone castles and fortifications, to defend against a possible second Mongol invasion. The [Mongols returned to Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Mongol_invasion_of_Hungary "Second Mongol invasion of Hungary") in 1285, but the newly built stone-castle systems and new tactics (using a higher proportion of heavily armed knights) stopped them. The invading Mongol force was defeated[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-66) near Pest by the royal army of King [Ladislaus IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ladislaus_IV_of_Hungary "Ladislaus IV of Hungary"). As with later invasions, it was repelled handily, the Mongols losing much of their invading force.

#### Age of elected kings

Main articles: [Kingdom of Hungary (1301–1526)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hungary_(1301%E2%80%931526) "Kingdom of Hungary (1301–1526)") and [Ottoman–Hungarian Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman%E2%80%93Hungarian_Wars "Ottoman–Hungarian Wars")

The [Kingdom of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hungary "Kingdom of Hungary") reached one of its greatest extents during the Árpádian kings, yet royal power was weakened at the end of their rule in 1301. After a destructive period of [interregnum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interregnum "Interregnum") (1301–1308), the first [Angevin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capetian_House_of_Anjou "Capetian House of Anjou") king, [Charles I of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_Hungary "Charles I of Hungary") – a bilineal descendant of the [Árpád dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%81rp%C3%A1d_dynasty "Árpád dynasty") – successfully restored royal power and defeated oligarch rivals, the so-called "little kings". The second Angevin Hungarian king, [Louis the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_I_of_Hungary "Louis I of Hungary") (1342–1382), led many successful military campaigns from Lithuania to southern Italy ([Kingdom of Naples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Naples "Kingdom of Naples")) and was also [King of Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Polish_monarchs "List of Polish monarchs") from 1370. After King Louis died without a male heir, the country was stabilised only when [Sigismund of Luxembourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigismund,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Sigismund, Holy Roman Emperor") (1387–1437) succeeded to the throne, who in 1433 also became [Holy Roman Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Emperor "Holy Roman Emperor"). The first Hungarian [Bible translation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible_translations "Bible translations") was completed in 1439. For half a year in 1437, there was an antifeudal and anticlerical [peasant revolt in Transylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transylvanian_peasant_revolt "Transylvanian peasant revolt") which was strongly influenced by [Hussite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hussite "Hussite") ideas. From a small noble family in Transylvania, [John Hunyadi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hunyadi "John Hunyadi") grew to become one of the country's most powerful lords, thanks to his capabilities as a mercenary commander. He was elected governor, then regent. He was a successful crusader against the [Ottoman Turks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Turks "Ottoman Turks"), one of his greatest victories being the [siege of Belgrade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Belgrade_(1456) "Siege of Belgrade (1456)") in 1456.

[![Image 19: Portrait, Matthias Corvinus, King of Hungary, Hunyadi, relief](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/Portrait_of_Matthias_Corvinus%2C_King_of_Hungary.jpg/250px-Portrait_of_Matthias_Corvinus%2C_King_of_Hungary.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Portrait_of_Matthias_Corvinus,_King_of_Hungary.jpg)

Renaissance portrait of [Matthias Corvinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthias_Corvinus "Matthias Corvinus"), King of Hungary and Croatia (1458–1490), King of Bohemia (1469–1490) and Archduke of Austria (1487–1490)

The last strong king of medieval Hungary was the [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance "Renaissance") king [Matthias Corvinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthias_Corvinus "Matthias Corvinus") (1458–1490), son of John Hunyadi. His election was the first time that a member of the nobility mounted the Hungarian royal throne without a dynastic background. He was a successful military leader and an enlightened patron of the arts and learning.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-britannica1-67) His library, the [Bibliotheca Corviniana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bibliotheca_Corviniana "Bibliotheca Corviniana"), was Europe's greatest collection of historical chronicles, philosophic and scientific works in the 15th century, and second only in size to the [Vatican Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vatican_Library "Vatican Library"). Items from the Bibliotheca Corviniana were inscribed on [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO")'s [Memory of the World Register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_of_the_World_Programme "Memory of the World Programme") in 2005.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-68) The serfs and common people considered him a just ruler because he protected them from excessive demands and other abuses by the magnates.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-69) Under his rule, in 1479, the Hungarian army destroyed the Ottoman and Wallachian troops at the [Battle of Breadfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Breadfield "Battle of Breadfield"). Abroad, he defeated the Polish and German imperial armies of Frederick at Breslau ([Wrocław](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wroc%C5%82aw "Wrocław")). Matthias' mercenary standing army, the [Black Army of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Army_of_Hungary "Black Army of Hungary"), was an unusually large army for its time, and it conquered [Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna "Vienna") as well as parts of Austria and [Bohemia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohemia "Bohemia").

King Matthias died without lawful sons, and the Hungarian magnates procured the accession of the Pole [Vladislaus II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladislaus_II_of_Hungary "Vladislaus II of Hungary") (1490–1516), supposedly because of his weak influence on Hungarian aristocracy.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-britannica1-67) Hungary's international role declined, its political stability was shaken, and social progress was deadlocked.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-70) In 1514, the weakened old King Vladislaus II faced a major peasant rebellion led by [György Dózsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gy%C3%B6rgy_D%C3%B3zsa "György Dózsa"), which was ruthlessly crushed by the [nobles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_nobility "Hungarian nobility"), led by [John Zápolya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Z%C3%A1polya "John Zápolya"). The resulting degradation of order paved the way for Ottoman preeminence. In 1521, the strongest Hungarian fortress in the South, Nándorfehérvár (today's [Belgrade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgrade "Belgrade"), Serbia), [fell to the Turks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Belgrade_(1521) "Siege of Belgrade (1521)"). The early appearance of Protestantism further worsened internal relations in the country.

### Ottoman wars (1526–1699)

Main articles: [Kingdom of Hungary (1526–1867)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hungary_(1526%E2%80%931867) "Kingdom of Hungary (1526–1867)"), [Ottoman Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Hungary "Ottoman Hungary"), and [Eastern Hungarian Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Hungarian_Kingdom "Eastern Hungarian Kingdom")

See also: [Principality of Transylvania (1570–1711)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principality_of_Transylvania_(1570%E2%80%931711) "Principality of Transylvania (1570–1711)") and [Ottoman–Habsburg wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman%E2%80%93Habsburg_wars "Ottoman–Habsburg wars")

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Sz%C3%A9kely%2C_Bertalan_-_The_Women_of_Eger_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg/250px-Sz%C3%A9kely%2C_Bertalan_-_The_Women_of_Eger_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sz%C3%A9kely,_Bertalan_-_The_Women_of_Eger_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg)

"The Women of Eger", oil painting from 1867 commemorating the [siege of Eger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Eger_(1552) "Siege of Eger (1552)"), a major victory against the Ottomans

After some [150 years of wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_wars_in_Europe "Ottoman wars in Europe") with the Hungarians and other states, the Ottomans gained a decisive victory over the Hungarian army at the [Battle of Mohács](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Moh%C3%A1cs "Battle of Mohács") in 1526, where King [Louis II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_II_of_Hungary "Louis II of Hungary") died while fleeing. Amid political chaos, the divided Hungarian nobility elected two kings simultaneously, [John Zápolya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Z%C3%A1polya "John Zápolya") and [Ferdinand I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_I,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor") of the [Habsburg dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Habsburg "House of Habsburg"). With the conquest of [Buda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buda "Buda") by the Turks in 1541, Hungary was divided into three parts and remained so until the end of the 17th century. The north-western part, termed as [Royal Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Hungary "Royal Hungary"), was annexed by the Habsburgs, who ruled as kings of Hungary. The eastern part of the kingdom became independent as the [Principality of Transylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principality_of_Transylvania_(1570%E2%80%931711) "Principality of Transylvania (1570–1711)"), under Ottoman (and later Habsburg) [suzerainty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suzerainty "Suzerainty"). The remaining central area, including the capital Buda, was known as the Pashalik of Buda.

In 1686, the [Holy League's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_League_(1684) "Holy League (1684)") army, containing over 74,000 men from various nations, [reconquered Buda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Buda_(1686) "Siege of Buda (1686)") from the Turks. After some more crushing [defeats of the Ottomans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austro-Turkish_War_(1716%E2%80%931718) "Austro-Turkish War (1716–1718)") in the next few years, the entire Kingdom of Hungary was removed from Ottoman rule by 1718. The last raid into Hungary by the Ottoman vassals [Tatars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimean_Khanate "Crimean Khanate") from [Crimea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimea "Crimea") took place in 1717.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-71) The constrained Habsburg Counter-Reformation efforts in the 17th century reconverted the majority of the kingdom to Catholicism. The ethnic composition of Hungary was fundamentally changed as a consequence of the prolonged warfare with the Turks. A large part of the country became devastated, population growth was stunted, and many smaller settlements perished.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-72) The Austrian-Habsburg government settled large groups of [Serbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbs "Serbs") and other Slavs in the depopulated south, and settled [Germans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germans_of_Hungary "Germans of Hungary") (called [Danube Swabians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danube_Swabians "Danube Swabians")) in various areas, but Hungarians were not allowed to settle or re-settle in the south of the Carpathian Basin.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-73)

### From the 18th century to World War I (1699–1918)

Main articles: [Rákóczi's War of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%A1k%C3%B3czi's_War_of_Independence "Rákóczi's War of Independence"), [Hungarian Reform Era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Reform_Era "Hungarian Reform Era"), [Hungarian Revolution of 1848](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Revolution_of_1848 "Hungarian Revolution of 1848"), [Lands of the Crown of Saint Stephen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lands_of_the_Crown_of_Saint_Stephen "Lands of the Crown of Saint Stephen"), and [Hungary in World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary_in_World_War_I "Hungary in World War I")

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/M%C3%A1nyoki%2C_%C3%81dam_-_Portrait_of_Prince_Ferenc_R%C3%A1k%C3%B3czi_II_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg/250px-M%C3%A1nyoki%2C_%C3%81dam_-_Portrait_of_Prince_Ferenc_R%C3%A1k%C3%B3czi_II_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:M%C3%A1nyoki,_%C3%81dam_-_Portrait_of_Prince_Ferenc_R%C3%A1k%C3%B3czi_II_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg)

[Francis II Rákóczi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_II_R%C3%A1k%C3%B3czi "Francis II Rákóczi"), leader of the war of independence against Habsburg rule (1703–1711)

Between 1703 and 1711, there was a large-scale [war of independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%A1k%C3%B3czi's_War_of_Independence "Rákóczi's War of Independence") led by [Francis II Rákóczi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_II_R%C3%A1k%C3%B3czi "Francis II Rákóczi"), who after the dethronement of the Habsburgs in 1707 at the Diet of [Ónod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%93nod "Ónod"), took power provisionally as the ruling prince for the wartime period, but refused the Hungarian crown and the title "king". The uprisings lasted for years. The Hungarian [Kuruc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuruc "Kuruc") army, although taking over most of the country, lost the main [battle at Trencsén](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Tren%C4%8D%C3%ADn "Battle of Trenčín") (1708). Three years later, because of the growing desertion, defeatism, and low morale, the Kuruc forces surrendered.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-74)

During the [Napoleonic Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleonic_Wars "Napoleonic Wars") and afterward, the Hungarian Diet had not convened for decades.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-75) In the 1820s, the emperor was forced to convene the Diet, which marked the beginning of a Reform Period (1825–1848, [Hungarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_language "Hungarian language"): _reformkor_). The Hungarian Parliament was reconvened in 1825 to handle financial needs. A liberal party emerged and focused on providing for the peasantry. [Lajos Kossuth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lajos_Kossuth "Lajos Kossuth") emerged as a leader of the lower [gentry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentry "Gentry") in the Parliament. [Lajos Kossuth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lajos_Kossuth "Lajos Kossuth"), Regent-President during the [Hungarian Revolution of 1848](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Revolution_of_1848 "Hungarian Revolution of 1848")

On 15 March 1848, mass demonstrations in Pest and Buda enabled Hungarian reformists to push through a list of [12 demands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/12_points_of_the_Hungarian_Revolutionaries_of_1848 "12 points of the Hungarian Revolutionaries of 1848"). The Habsburg ruler and his advisors skillfully manipulated the Croatian, Serbian and Romanian peasantry, led by priests and officers firmly loyal to the Habsburgs, into rebelling against the Hungarian government, though the Hungarians were supported by the vast majority of the Slovak, German and [Rusyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rusyns "Rusyns") nationalities and by all the Jews of the kingdom, as well as by a large number of Polish, Austrian and Italian volunteers.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-76) In July 1849, the Hungarian Parliament proclaimed and enacted the first laws of ethnic and [minority rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_rights "Minority rights") in the world.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-77) Many members of minority nationalities, like [János Damjanich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%A1nos_Damjanich "János Damjanich") and [Józef Bem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%B3zef_Bem "Józef Bem"), gained the coveted highest positions within the Hungarian Army. The Hungarian forces (_[Honvédség](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal\_Hungarian\_Landwehr "Royal Hungarian Landwehr")_) defeated the Austrian armies. To counter the successes of the Hungarian revolutionary army, Habsburg Emperor [Franz Joseph I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz_Joseph_I_of_Austria "Franz Joseph I of Austria") asked for help from the "Gendarme of Europe", Tsar [Nicholas I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_I_of_Russia "Nicholas I of Russia"), whose Russian armies invaded Hungary. This made [Artúr Görgey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art%C3%BAr_G%C3%B6rgei "Artúr Görgei") surrender in August 1849. The leader of the Austrian army, [Julius Jacob von Haynau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Jacob_von_Haynau "Julius Jacob von Haynau"), became governor of Hungary for a few months and ordered the execution of [the 13 Martyrs of Arad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_13_Martyrs_of_Arad "The 13 Martyrs of Arad"), leaders of the Hungarian army, and Prime Minister Batthyány in October 1849. Kossuth escaped into exile. Following the war of 1848–1849, the whole country was in "passive resistance".

Because of external and internal problems, reforms seemed inevitable, and major military defeats of Austria forced the Habsburgs to negotiate the [Austro-Hungarian Compromise of 1867](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austro-Hungarian_Compromise_of_1867 "Austro-Hungarian Compromise of 1867"), by which the dual monarchy of [Austria-Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria-Hungary "Austria-Hungary") was formed. This empire had the second largest area in Europe (after the [Russian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Empire "Russian Empire")), and it was the third most populous (after Russia and the [German Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Empire "German Empire")). The two realms were governed separately by two parliaments from two capital cities, with a common monarch and common external and military policies. Economically, the empire was a customs union. The old Hungarian Constitution was restored, and Franz Joseph I was crowned as [King of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_Hungary "King of Hungary"). The era witnessed impressive economic development. The formerly backward Hungarian economy became relatively modern and industrialised by the turn of the 20th century, although agriculture remained dominant until 1890.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-78) In 1873, the old capital Buda and [Óbuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%93buda "Óbuda") were officially united with [Pest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pest,_Hungary "Pest, Hungary"),[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-79) creating the new metropolis of Budapest.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-80)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary#cite_note-81) Many of the state institutions and the modern administrative system of Hungary were established during this period.

The [Lands of the Crown of Saint Stephen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lands_of_the_Crown_of_Saint_Stephen "Lands of the Crown of Saint Stephen") consisted of the territories of the [Kingdom of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hungary "Kingdom of Hungary") (16) and the [Kingdom of Croatia-Slavonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Croatia-Slavonia "Kingdom of Croatia-Slavonia") (17).

Austria-Hungary drafted over 4 million soldiers from the Kingdom of Hungary on the side of Germany, Bulgaria, and Turkey. The [Eastern Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Front_(World_War_I) "Eastern Front (World War I)") of the Allied ([Entente](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_I "Allies of World War I")) Powers completely collapsed. The **economy of Hungary** is a [developing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Developing_country "Developing country"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-devgroup-1) high-income [mixed economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_economy "Mixed economy") that is the [53rd-largest economy in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP) "List of countries by GDP (PPP)") (out of 188 countries measured by [IMF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMF "IMF")) with $265.037 billion annual output,[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-imf2-29) and ranks [41st in the world in terms of GDP per capita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP)_per_capita "List of countries by GDP (PPP) per capita") measured by [purchasing power parity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purchasing_power_parity "Purchasing power parity"). Hungary has a [very high human development index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_Human_Development_Index "List of countries by Human Development Index") and a skilled [labour force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_force "Labour force"), with the [22nd lowest income inequality by Gini index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_income_equality "List of countries by income equality") in the world. Hungary has an export-oriented [market economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_economy "Market economy") with a heavy emphasis on [foreign trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_trade "Foreign trade"); thus the country is the [35th largest export economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_exports "List of countries by exports") in the world. The country had more than $100 billion of exports in 2015, with a high [trade surplus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_surplus "Trade surplus") of $9.003 billion, of which 79% went to the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") (EU) and 21% was extra-EU trade.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-30) Hungary's productive capacity is more than 80% [privately owned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_sector "Private sector"), with [39.1% overall taxation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_tax_revenue_as_percentage_of_GDP "List of countries by tax revenue as percentage of GDP"), which funds the country's [welfare economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welfare_state "Welfare state").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] On the expenditure side, [household consumption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Household_consumption "Household consumption") is the main component of [GDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GDP "GDP") and accounts for 50% of its total, followed by gross fixed [capital formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_formation "Capital formation") with 22% and [government expenditure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_expenditure "Government expenditure") with 20%.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-31)

In 2015 Hungary attracted $119.8 billion in [FDI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_direct_investment "Foreign direct investment") and invested more than $50 billion abroad.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-32) As of 2015, the key trading partners of Hungary were Germany, Austria, Romania, Slovakia, France, Italy, Poland and the Czech Republic.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-33) Major industries include food processing, pharmaceuticals, motor vehicles, information technology, chemicals, metallurgy, machinery, electrical goods, and tourism (in 2014 Hungary received 12.1 million international tourists).[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-34) Hungary is the largest electronics producer in [Central and Eastern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_and_Eastern_Europe "Central and Eastern Europe"). [Electronics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronics "Electronics") manufacturing and research are among the main drivers of [innovation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Innovation "Innovation") and economic growth in the country. In the past 20 years Hungary has also grown into a major center for [mobile technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_technology "Mobile technology"), [information security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_security "Information security"), and related hardware research.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-35)

The [employment rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Employment_rate "Employment rate") in the economy was 68.7% in January 2017,[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-ksh.hu-36) while the employment structure shows the characteristics of [post-industrial economies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-industrial_society "Post-industrial society"). An estimated 63.2% of the employed workforce work in the service sector, industry contributed by 29.7%, while agriculture employed 7.1%. The unemployment rate was 3.8% in September–November 2017,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-ReferenceA-37) down from 11% during the [Great Recession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Recession "Great Recession"). Hungary is part of the [European single market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_single_market "European single market"), which represents more than 448 million consumers. Several domestic commercial policies are determined by agreements among European Union members and by EU legislation.

Large [Hungarian companies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_companies_of_Hungary "List of companies of Hungary") are included in the [BUX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BUX "BUX"), the Hungarian stock market index listed on [Budapest Stock Exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budapest_Stock_Exchange "Budapest Stock Exchange"). Well-known companies include [Graphisoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphisoft "Graphisoft"), [Magyar Telekom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magyar_Telekom "Magyar Telekom"), [MBH Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBH_Bank "MBH Bank"), [MOL Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MOL_Group "MOL Group"), [Opus Global](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opus_Global "Opus Global"), [OTP Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OTP_Bank "OTP Bank"), [RÁBA Automotive Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%A1ba_(company) "Rába (company)"), [Gedeon Richter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gedeon_Richter_(company) "Gedeon Richter (company)") and [Zwack Unicum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zwack "Zwack"). Hungary also has a large number of specialised [small and medium enterprises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small_and_medium_enterprise "Small and medium enterprise"), for example many automotive industry suppliers and technology [start ups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Startup_company "Startup company").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-38)

[Budapest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budapest "Budapest") is the financial and business capital of Hungary. The capital is a significant economic hub, classified as an Beta [world city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_city "World city") in the study by the [Globalization and World Cities Research Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Globalization_and_World_Cities_Research_Network "Globalization and World Cities Research Network") and it is the second fastest-developing [urban economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_economy "Urban economy") in Europe. The per capita GDP in the city increased by 2.4% and employment by 4.7% compared to the previous year, 2014.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-39) On the national level, Budapest is the [primary city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primate_city "Primate city") of Hungary for business, accounting for 39% of the national income. The city had a [gross metropolitan product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_metropolitan_product "Gross metropolitan product") of more than $100 billion in 2015, making it one of the largest regional economies in the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-41) Budapest is also among the top 100 GDP performing cities in the world, as measured by [PricewaterhouseCoopers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PricewaterhouseCoopers "PricewaterhouseCoopers"). In a global city competitiveness ranking by the [Economist Intelligence Unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economist_Intelligence_Unit "Economist Intelligence Unit"), Budapest is ranked above [Tel Aviv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tel_Aviv "Tel Aviv"), [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon"), [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow") and [Johannesburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannesburg "Johannesburg"), among others.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-43)

Hungary maintains its own currency, the [Hungarian forint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_forint "Hungarian forint") (HUF), although the economy fulfills the [Maastricht criteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maastricht_criteria "Maastricht criteria") with the exception of public debt. The ratio of public debt to GDP is [significantly below the EU average](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_public_debt "List of countries by public debt") at 66.4% in 2019. The [Hungarian National Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_National_Bank "Hungarian National Bank") was founded in 1924, after the dissolution of the [Austro-Hungarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austro-Hungarian_Empire "Austro-Hungarian Empire"). It is currently focusing on price stability, with an inflation target of 3%.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-44)

The economy of Hungary is a high-income mixed economy, and a member of the European Union's single market. In recent years, it has become one of the faster-growing economies in the EU, transitioning towards an export-oriented market economy with a strong focus on foreign trade and investment, particularly in the automotive and electronics sectors.

According to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Hungary's estimated annual output was $219 billion (nominal GDP) in 2024, ranking it as the 57th-largest economy in the world. In terms of GDP per capita measured by purchasing power parity (PPP), it ranked 42nd globally at approximately $47,213.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-IMF_WEO_Apr20242-45)

Hungary maintains a very high Human Development Index, ranking 47th in the 2023/24 report, and possesses a skilled labour force.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-46) The country has one of the lowest income inequalities in the EU, with a Gini coefficient of 29.6 in 2023.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-47) The economy is heavily reliant on exports, primarily to other EU nations. In 2023, its goods exports reached €149.2 billion, generating a significant trade surplus of €9.8 billion.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-48) On the expenditure side, household consumption accounts for approximately 50% of GDP, followed by gross fixed capital formation (26%) and government expenditure (18%).[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-49)

Key industries include automobile manufacturing, battery production, electronics, pharmaceuticals, and information technology. After facing the highest inflation in the EU in 2023 (averaging 17.1%), policy measures successfully brought the rate down to a forecasted 3.5% for 2025.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-IMF_WEO_Apr20242-45) The unemployment rate remained low at 4.1% in early 2025, while the government debt-to-GDP ratio was projected to be around 72.0%.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-IMF_WEO_Apr20242-45) Budapest, the capital, serves as the nation's primary financial and business hub.

### Árpád Age

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Hungary&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Árpád Age")]

In the age of [feudalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudalism "Feudalism") the key economic factor was land. The new economic and social orders created private ownership of land. There are three forms of existence[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_]: the royal, ecclesiastical and secular private estate. The royal estate of the [Árpád dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%81rp%C3%A1d_dynasty "Árpád dynasty") had evolved from the tribal lands.[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_]

The origin of the secular private holdings dates back to the conquest tribal common estates[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_], which are increasingly in charge of the society and grows over private ownership of the becoming leaders.

However, from the founding of the state the royal gift also entered the multiplying factors secular private property line. This organization developed a feudal estate, which had two elements: the ancient estate and the possessions which were awarded by [Saint Stephen I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Stephen_I "Saint Stephen I"), and then the royal donations. [Béla III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9la_III "Béla III") was the wealthiest European monarch of his time, according to [a list of his revenues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Income_register_of_B%C3%A9la_III_of_Hungary "Income register of Béla III of Hungary"), but the reliability of the list is questioned. Over the holder unrestricted right granted by the latter lineal heir almost returned to the king. In the Order of the laws changed in 1351, which abolished the nobility's possessions for free disposal. It forbidden the nobility to sale their inherited land.

The [Carpathian Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carpathian_Basin "Carpathian Basin") was more suitable for agriculture than large livestock grazing, and therefore increased steadily in the former weight. In the 11th and 12th centuries natural farming and soil changer tillage systems met: grazing the animals, and they used the fertilized land until depletion. The most important tools for the agriculture were the plow and the ox.

The Hungarian economy prior to [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") was primarily oriented toward agriculture and small-scale manufacturing. Hungary's strategic position in [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe") and its relative high lack of natural resources also have dictated a traditional reliance on foreign trade. For instance, its largest car manufacturer, [Magomobil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magomobil "Magomobil") (maker of the _Magosix_), produced a total of a few thousand units.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-50) In the early 1920s the textile industry began to expand rapidly, by 1928 it became the most important industry in the foreign trade of Hungary exporting textile goods worth more than 60 million pengős in that year. Companies like [MÁVAG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%81VAG "MÁVAG") exported locomotives to [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India") and [South-America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South-America "South-America"), its [locomotive no. 601](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%81V_Class_601 "MÁV Class 601") was the largest and most powerful in [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe") at the time.

### Post-war Hungarian communism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Hungary&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Post-war Hungarian communism")]

Further information: [Hungarian People's Republic §Economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_People's_Republic#Economy "Hungarian People's Republic"), and [Goulash Communism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goulash_Communism "Goulash Communism")

From the late 1940s, the [Communist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist "Communist") government started to nationalize the industry. At first, only factories with more than 100 workers were nationalized; later, this limit was reduced to only 10. In the agriculture, the government started a successful program of [collectivization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collectivization_in_Hungary "Collectivization in Hungary"). From the early 1950s, more and more new factories were built. This rapid and forced industrialization followed the standard [Stalinist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stalinist "Stalinist") pattern in an effort to encourage a more self-sufficient economy. Most economic activity was conducted by state-owned enterprises or cooperatives and state farms. In 1968, [Stalinist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stalinist "Stalinist") self-sufficiency was replaced by the "[New Economic Mechanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Economic_Mechanism "New Economic Mechanism")", which reopened Hungary to foreign trade, gave limited freedom to the workings of the market, and allowed a limited number of small businesses to operate in the services sector.

In this era great social progress was made, for example the population between 20 and 24 years old with less than 8 years of education decreased from 71.2% in 1949 to 4.9% in 1984, the annual consumption of meat and fish increased from 35 kilograms in 1950 to 78 in 1984, the percentage of homes with electricity increased from 46.6% in 1949 to 99% in 1984, in the same period the percentage of homes with running water increased from 17.1% to 76.6%, the number of cars per 1,000 people increased from 3 in 1960 to 122 in 1984, in the case of televisions from 10 to 276, in the case of washing machines from 45 to 317, in the case of refrigerators from 4 to 328, infant mortality (per 1,000 live births) fell from 91 in 1949 to 20.4 in 1984.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-auto3-51)

Per capita national income grew by 343% from 1950 to 1983 (4.6% per year), real wages by 136% and real incomes by 251% over the same period, meanwhile real value of per capita social benefits rose by 432% from 1960 to 1980. From 1949 to 1984, Hungary's GDP grew as fast as that of countries like Spain.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-auto3-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-53)

Also poverty was greatly reduced, although from 1962 to 1982 the price index rose by 96%, people with less than 800 forints were 55% in 1962 and after 20 years only 6.4% of those with less than 1800 forints. In 1987, inequality was minimal, with a Gini coefficient of 0.21, and poverty was the same, with a 1% poverty rate (poverty line: $120 PPP per person per month).[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-auto3-51)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-54)

Although Hungary enjoyed one of the most liberal and economically advanced economies of the former [Eastern Bloc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Bloc "Eastern Bloc") even though at the end of the 1980s state employment represented 94% of the total, both agriculture and industry began to suffer from a lack of investment in the 1970s, and Hungary's net foreign debt rose significantly—from $1 billion in 1973 to $15 billion in 1993—due largely to consumer subsidies and unprofitable state enterprises. In the face of economic stagnation, Hungary opted to liberalize further by passing a joint venture law, instating an income tax, and joining the [International Monetary Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Monetary_Fund "International Monetary Fund") ([IMF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMF "IMF")) and the [World Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Bank "World Bank"). By 1988, Hungary had developed a [two-tier banking system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-tier_banking_system "Two-tier banking system"), and had enacted significant corporate legislation that paved the way for the ambitious market-oriented reforms of the post-communist years.

### Transition to a market economy (1990–1995)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Hungary&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Transition to a market economy (1990–1995)")]

[![Image 46](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/ING-Bank-szekhaz-P2030395-lev-1000.jpg/250px-ING-Bank-szekhaz-P2030395-lev-1000.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ING-Bank-szekhaz-P2030395-lev-1000.jpg)

ING headquarters in Budapest

After the fall of communism, the former Eastern Bloc had to transition from a one-party, centrally [planned economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_economy "Planned economy") to a market economy with a [multi-party political system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-party_political_system "Multi-party political system"). With the [collapse of the Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collapse_of_the_Soviet_Union "Collapse of the Soviet Union"), the Eastern Bloc countries suffered a significant loss in both markets for goods, and subsidizing from the Soviet Union.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-55) Hungary, for example, "lost nearly 70% of its export markets in Eastern and Central Europe." The loss of external markets in Hungary left "800,000 unemployed people because all the unprofitable and unsalvageable factories had been closed."[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-es-56) Another form of Soviet subsidizing that greatly affected Hungary after the fall of communism was the loss of social welfare programs. Because of the lack of subsidies and a need to reduce expenditures, many social programs in Hungary had to be cut in an attempt to lower spending. As a result, many people in Hungary suffered incredible hardships during the transition to a market economy. Following [privatization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privatization "Privatization") and tax reductions on Hungarian businesses, unemployment suddenly rose to 12% in 1991 (it was 1.7% in 1990 ), gradually decreasing until 2001. Economic growth, after a fall in 1991 to −11.9%, gradually grew until the end of the 1990s at an average annual rate of 4.2%. With the stabilization of the new market economy Hungary experienced growth in [foreign investment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_direct_investment "Foreign direct investment"),[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-megginson01-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-mihalyi01-58) with a "cumulative foreign direct investment totaling more than $60 billion since 1989."[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-59)

The [Antall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antall "Antall") government of 1990–94 began market reforms with price and trade liberation measures, a revamped tax system, and a nascent market-based banking system. By 1994, however, the costs of government overspending and hesitant privatization had become clearly visible. Cuts in consumer subsidies led to increases in the price of food, medicine, transportation services, and energy. Reduced exports to the former Soviet bloc and shrinking industrial output contributed to a sharp decline in GDP. Unemployment rose rapidly to about 12% in 1993. The external debt burden, one of the highest in Europe, reached 250% of annual export earnings, while the budget and current account deficits approached 10% of GDP. The [devaluation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devaluation "Devaluation") of the currency (in order to support exports), without effective stabilization measures, such as [indexation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indexation "Indexation") of wages, provoked an extremely high inflation rate, that in 1991 reached 35% and slightly decreased until 1994, growing again in 1995. In March 1995, the government of Prime Minister [Gyula Horn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyula_Horn "Gyula Horn") implemented an austerity program, coupled with aggressive privatization of state-owned enterprises and an export-promoting exchange raw regime, to reduce indebtedness, cut the current account deficit, and shrink public spending. By the end of 1997 the consolidated public sector deficit decreased to 4.6% of GDP—with public sector spending falling from 62% of GDP to below 50%—the current account deficit was reduced to 2% of GDP, and government debt was paid down to 94% of annual export earnings.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

[![Image 47](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Megyeri_h%C3%ADd.jpg/250px-Megyeri_h%C3%ADd.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Megyeri_h%C3%ADd.jpg)

[Megyeri Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megyeri_Bridge "Megyeri Bridge")

The Government of Hungary no longer requires IMF financial assistance and has repaid all of its debt to the fund. Consequently, Hungary enjoys favorable borrowing terms. Hungary's sovereign foreign currency debt issuance carries investment-grade ratings from all major credit-rating agencies, although recently the country was downgraded by Moody's, S&P and remains on negative outlook at Fitch. In 1995 Hungary's currency, the Forint (HUF), became convertible for all current account transactions, and subsequent to [OECD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OECD "OECD") membership in 1996, for almost all capital account transactions as well. Since 1995, Hungary has pegged the forint against a basket of currencies (in which the U.S. dollar is 30%), and the central rate against the basket is devalued at a preannounced rate, originally set at 0.8% per month, the Forint is now an entirely free-floating currency. The government privatization program ended on schedule in 1998: 80% of GDP is now produced by the private sector,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-:0-14) and foreign owners control 70% of financial institutions, 66% of industry, 90% of telecommunications, and 50% of the trading sector.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

[![Image 48](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/K%C5%91r%C3%B6shegy_l%C3%A9gifot%C3%B3.jpg/250px-K%C5%91r%C3%B6shegy_l%C3%A9gifot%C3%B3.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:K%C5%91r%C3%B6shegy_l%C3%A9gifot%C3%B3.jpg)

Kőröshegy Viaduct

After Hungary's GDP declined about 18% from 1990 to 1993 and grew only 1%–1.5% up to 1996, strong [export performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Export_performance "Export performance") propelled GDP growth to 4.4% in 1997, with other macroeconomic indicators similarly improving. These successes allowed the government to concentrate in 1996 and 1997 on major structural reforms such as the implementation of a fully funded pension system (partly modelled after [Chile's pension system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chile_pension_system "Chile pension system") with major modifications), reform of higher education, and the creation of a national treasury. Remaining economic challenges include reducing fiscal deficits and inflation, maintaining stable external balances, and completing structural reforms of the tax system, health care, and local government financing. Recently, the overriding goal of Hungarian economic policy has been to prepare the country for entry into the European Union, which it joined in late 2004.

Prior to the change of regime in 1989, 65% of Hungary's trade was with [Comecon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comecon "Comecon") countries. By the end of 1997, Hungary had shifted much of its trade to the West. Trade with EU countries now comprises 80% of the total.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-:1-60) Germany is Hungary's single most important trading partner. The US has become Hungary's sixth-largest export market, while Hungary is ranked as the 72nd largest export market for the U.S. Bilateral trade between the two countries increased 46% in 1997 to more than $1 billion. The U.S. has extended to Hungary most-favored-nation status, the Generalized System of Preferences, Overseas Private Investment Corporation insurance, and access to the [Export-Import Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Export-Import_Bank_of_the_United_States "Export-Import Bank of the United States").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

With about $18 billion in foreign direct investment (FDI) since 1989, Hungary has attracted over one-third of all FDI in central and eastern Europe, including the former Soviet Union. Of this, about $6 billion came from American companies. Foreign capital is attracted by skilled and relatively inexpensive labor, tax incentives, modern infrastructure, and a good telecommunications system.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-61)

By 2006 Hungary's economic outlook had deteriorated. Wage growth had kept up with other nations in the region; however, this growth has largely been driven by increased government spending. This resulted in the budget deficit ballooning to over 10% of GDP and inflation rates predicted to exceed 6%. [Nouriel Roubini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nouriel_Roubini "Nouriel Roubini"), an economist in the Clinton administration, said that "Hungary is an accident waiting to happen."[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-62)

### Privatization

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Hungary&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Privatization")]

In January 1990, the State Privatization Agency (SPA, _Állami Vagyonügynökség_) was established to manage the first steps of [privatization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privatization "Privatization"). Because of Hungary's $21.2 billion [foreign debt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_debt "Foreign debt"), the government decided to sell state property instead of distributing it to the people for free.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-3541privatization_in_hun-63) The SPA was attacked by populist groups because several companies' management had the right to find buyers and discuss sale terms with them thus "stealing" the company. Another reason for discontent was that the state offered large tax subsidies and environmental investments, which sometimes cost more than the selling price of the company. Along with the acquisition of companies, foreign investors launched many "greenfield investments".[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-3541privatization_in_hun-63)

The center-right [Hungarian Democratic Forum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Democratic_Forum "Hungarian Democratic Forum") government of 1990–1994 decided to abolish agricultural co-operatives by splitting them up and giving machinery and land to their former members.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-3458strucutural_problems-64) The government also introduced a Recompensation Law which offered vouchers to people who had owned land before it was nationalized in 1948. These people (or their descendants) could exchange their vouchers for land previously owned by agricultural co-operatives, who were forced to give up some of their land for this purpose.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-3458strucutural_problems-64)

Small stores and retail businesses were privatized between 1990 and 1994, however, [greenfield investments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenfield_investment "Greenfield investment") by foreign retail companies like [Tesco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tesco "Tesco"), [Cora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cora_(hypermarket) "Cora (hypermarket)") and [IKEA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IKEA "IKEA") had a much bigger economic impact.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-3541privatization_in_hun-63) Many public utilities, including the national telecommunications company [Matáv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mat%C3%A1v "Matáv"), the national oil and gas conglomerate [MOL Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MOL_Group "MOL Group"), and electricity supply and production company [MVM Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MVM_Group "MVM Group") were privatized as well.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-4991privatisation_in_hun-65)

Though most banks were sold to foreign investors, the largest bank, [National Savings Bank (OTP)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OTP_Bank "OTP Bank"), remained Hungarian-owned. 20%–20% of the shares were sold to foreign institutional investors and given to the Social Security organizations, 5% were bought by employees, and 8% was offered at the [Budapest Stock Exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budapest_Stock_Exchange "Budapest Stock Exchange").[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-5955political_economy_of-66)
