Reaching 1995, Hungary's fiscal indices deteriorated: foreign investment fell as well as judgement of foreign analysts on economic outlook.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-bokrosinterview-67) Due to high demand in import goods, Hungary also had a high trade deficit[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-exttrade-68) and budget gap, and it could not reach an agreement with the [IMF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMF "IMF"), either.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-bokrosinterview-67)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-vg_hu-69) After not having a [minister of finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_finance "Minister of finance") for more than a month, prime minister [Gyula Horn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyula_Horn "Gyula Horn") appointed [Lajos Bokros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lajos_Bokros "Lajos Bokros") as Finance Minister on 1 March 1995. He introduced a string of austerity measures (the "[Bokros Package](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bokros_package "Bokros package")") on 12 March 1995 which had the following key points: one-time 9% devaluation of the forint, introducing a constant sliding devaluation, 8% additional customs duty on all goods except for energy sources, limitation of growth of wages in the public sector, simplified and accelerated privatization. The package also included welfare cutbacks, including abolition of free higher education and dental service; reduced family allowances, child-care benefits, and maternity payments depending on income and wealth; lowering subsidies of pharmaceuticals, and raising retirement age.

These reforms not only increased investor confidence,[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-usgovcikk-70) but they were also supported by the IMF and the World Bank,[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-konyv-71) however, they were not welcome widely by the Hungarians; Bokros broke the negative record of popularity: 9% of the population wanted to see him in an "important political position"[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-median_bokros-72) and only 4% were convinced that the reforms would "improve the country's finances in a big way"[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-bokrosinterview-67)

In 1996, the Ministry of Finance introduced a new pension system instead of the fully state-backed one: private pension savings accounts were introduced, which were 50% social security based and 50% funded.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-konyv-71)

In 2006 Prime Minister [Ferenc Gyurcsány](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferenc_Gyurcs%C3%A1ny "Ferenc Gyurcsány") was reelected on a platform promising economic "reform without austerity". However, after the elections in April 2006, the Socialist coalition under Gyurcsány unveiled a package of austerity measures which were designed to reduce the budget deficit to 3% of GDP by 2008.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-:2-73) Because of the austerity program, the economy of Hungary slowed down in 2007.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-:2-73)

### Great Recession

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Hungary&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Great Recession")]

Declining exports, reduced domestic consumption and fixed asset accumulation affected Hungary during the [Great Recession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Recession "Great Recession"), making the country enter a severe recession of −6.4%, one of the worst economic contractions in its history.

On 27 October 2008, Hungary reached an agreement with the [IMF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMF "IMF") and [EU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EU "EU") for a rescue package of US$25 billion, aiming to restore financial stability and investors' confidence.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-8078hungary_receives_res-74)

Because of the uncertainty of the crisis, banks gave less loans which led to a decrease in investment. This along with price-awareness and fear of bankruptcy led to a fallback in consumption which then increased job losses and decreased consumption even further. Inflation did not rise significantly, but real wages decreased.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-7679economy_and_society_-75)

The fact that the euro and the Swiss franc are worth a lot more in forints than they were before affected a lot of people. According to The Daily Telegraph, "statistics show that more than 60 percent of Hungarian mortgages and car loans are denominated in foreign currencies".[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-9940global_financial_cri-76) After the election in 2010 of the new [Fidesz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidesz "Fidesz")-party government of Prime Minister [Viktor Orbán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viktor_Orb%C3%A1n "Viktor Orbán"), Hungarian banks were forced to allow the conversion of foreign-currency mortgages to the forint.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-bloomberg-20111230-77) The new government also nationalized $13 billion of private pension-fund assets, which could then be used to support the government debt position.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-bloomberg-20111222-78)

### Post-recession

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Hungary&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Post-recession")]

The economy showed signs of recovery in 2011 with decreasing tax rates and a moderate 1.7 percent GDP growth.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-79)

From November 2011 to January 2012, all three major [credit rating agencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credit_rating_agencies "Credit rating agencies") downgraded Hungarian debt to a non-investment speculative grade, commonly called "junk status".[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-bbc-20111222-80)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-guardian-20111225-81)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-bbc-20120106-82) In part this is because of political changes creating doubts about the independence of the [Hungarian National Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_National_Bank "Hungarian National Bank").[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-83)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-bbc-20111222-80)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-guardian-20111225-81)

European Commission President [José Manuel Barroso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Manuel_Barroso "José Manuel Barroso") wrote to Prime Minister [Viktor Orbán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viktor_Orb%C3%A1n "Viktor Orbán") stating that new central bank regulations, allowing political intervention, "seriously harm" Hungary's interests, postponing talks on a financial aid package. Orbán responded "If we don't reach an agreement, we'll still stand on our own feet."[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-bloomberg-20111230-77)

The [European Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Commission "European Commission") launched legal proceedings against Hungary on 17 January 2012. The procedures concern Hungary's [central bank law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_National_Bank "Hungarian National Bank"), the retirement age for judges and prosecutors and the independence of the data protection office, respectively.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-84)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-85) One day later Orbán indicated in a letter his willingness to find solutions to the problems raised in the infringement proceedings.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-86) On 18 January he participated in plenary session of the [European Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Parliament "European Parliament") which also dealt with the Hungarian case. He said "Hungary has been renewed and reorganised under European principles". He also said that the problems raised by the European Union can be resolved "easily, simply and very quickly". He added that none of the EC's objections affected Hungary's new constitution.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-87)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-88)

Following the mild recession of 2012, the GDP picked up again from 2014, and based on the commission's Winter 2015 forecast it was projected to have accelerated to 3.3%. The more dynamic economic performance attributed to a moderately growing domestic demand and supported the growth of gross fixed capital formation. The surge (3.8% in the first half of 2014), however was only achieved via temporary measures and factors, such as the stepped-up absorption of EU-funds and the central bank's Funding for Growth Scheme, which subsidised loans for small-and medium-sized enterprises.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-89) The fundaments of growth didn't considerably change in 2015 as well – the government supported EU-fund transfers along with the moderately successful central bank loans of economic revitalization – fueled the fair GDP growth.

### During and after the COVID-19 pandemic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Hungary&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: During and after the COVID-19 pandemic")]

The Hungarian GDP, GDP per capita, living standards and wages had been steadily rising until the start of the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), when just like the rest of Europe, the stats above tanked. GDP fell to $155 billion, GDP PPP has fallen to $322 Billion, GDP per capita to $15,855, inflation slightly rose to 4.54%.

National debt rose considerably, to around 80% Debt-to-GDP from the previous 60–65%.

The country was hard hit, unemployment was also higher than average until 2021 when the lockdowns ended. The GDP, GDP per capita, GDP PPP, unemployment and national debt have all recovered to and beyond their pre-COVID values.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] On the other hand, [inflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflation "Inflation") has risen to the record levels, reaching 24.5% in December 2022, being the highest in Europe.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-90)

## Natural resources

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Hungary&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Natural resources")]

Main article: [Geography of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Hungary "Geography of Hungary")

[![Image 53](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c6/Hungary_topographic_map.jpg/250px-Hungary_topographic_map.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hungary_topographic_map.jpg)

Topographic map of Hungary

Hungary's total land area is 93,030 km 2 along with 690 km 2 of water surface area which altogether makes up 1% of Europe's area.

Nearly 75% of Hungary's landscape consists of flat plains. Additional 20% of the country's area consists of foothills whose altitude is 400 m at the most; higher hills and water surface makes up the remaining 5%.

The two flat plains that take up three-quarters of Hungary's area are the [Great Hungarian Plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Hungarian_Plain "Great Hungarian Plain") and the [Little Hungarian Plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Hungarian_Plain "Little Hungarian Plain"). Hungary's most significant natural resource is arable land. About 83% of the country's total territory is suitable for cultivation;[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-6601the_hungarian_agricu-91) of this portion, 75% (around 50% of the country's area) is covered by arable land, which is an outstanding ratio compared to other EU countries.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-6601the_hungarian_agricu-91) Hungary lacks extensive domestic sources of energy and raw materials needed for further industrial development.

19% of the country is covered by forests. These are located mainly in the foothills such as the [North Hungarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Hungarian_Mountains "North Hungarian Mountains") and the [Transdanubian Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transdanubian_Mountains "Transdanubian Mountains"), and the [Alpokalja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpokalja "Alpokalja"). The composition of forests is various; mostly oak or beech, but the rest include fir, willow, acacia and plane.

[![Image 54](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/Medicinal_Bath_H%C3%A9v%C3%ADz_01.jpg/250px-Medicinal_Bath_H%C3%A9v%C3%ADz_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Medicinal_Bath_H%C3%A9v%C3%ADz_01.jpg)

Medicinal bath in [Hévíz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9v%C3%ADz "Hévíz")

In European terms, Hungary's underground water reserve is one of the largest. Hence the country is rich in brooks and hot springs as well as medicinal springs and spas; as of 2003, there are 1250 springs that provide water warmer than 30°C.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-6827a_h_v_zfelt_r_s_te-92) 90% of Hungary's drinking water is mostly retrieved from such sources.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-6435magyarorsz_g_term_sz-93)

The major rivers of Hungary are the [Danube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danube "Danube") and the [Tisza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tisza "Tisza"). The Danube also flows through parts of [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany"), [Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria "Austria"), [Slovakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia "Slovakia"), [Serbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbia "Serbia"), and [Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romania "Romania"). It is navigable within Hungary for 418 km. The Tisza River is navigable for 444 km in the country. Hungary has three major lakes. [Lake Balaton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Balaton "Lake Balaton"), the largest, is 78 km long and from 3 to 14 km wide, with an area of 592 km 2. Lake Balaton is Central Europe's largest lake and a prosperous tourist spot and recreation area. Its shallow waters offer summer bathing and during the winter its frozen surface provides facilities for winter sports. Smaller bodies of water include [Lake Velence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Velence "Lake Velence") (26 km 2) in Fejér County and [Lake Fertő](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Fert%C5%91 "Lake Fertő") (82 km 2 within Hungary).

The waters of the country are in danger, since more water is going out of the county than in. In 2022, a severe drought which has impacted all of Europe is endangering among others, Lake Velence, Lake Balaton, the Danube and Tisza rivers. The flow of the aforementioned rivers have been modified in the late 19th century, and while it prevented larger floods and helped water transport, it has its downsides, such as the inability to support large-scale watering of crops, worsening the drought of 2022. Large-scale reforms and rebuilding of the Alföld water system is needed, but no such plans are being announced by the government as of 2022.

### Agriculture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Hungary&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Agriculture")]

See also: [Honey production in Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honey_production_in_Hungary "Honey production in Hungary") and [Hungarian wine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_wine "Hungarian wine")

[![Image 55](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/Tokaj_vineyard.jpg/250px-Tokaj_vineyard.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tokaj_vineyard.jpg)

[Tokaj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokaj-Hegyalja "Tokaj-Hegyalja") vineyard with ripening grapes

Agriculture accounted for 4.3% of GDP in 2008[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-1404value_and_distributi-95) and along with the food industry occupied roughly 7.7% of the labor force.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-7495number_of_employed_p-96) These two figures represent only the primary agricultural production: along with related businesses, agriculture makes up about 13% of the GDP.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-6601the_hungarian_agricu-91) Hungarian agriculture is virtually self-sufficient and due to traditional reasons export-oriented:[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-6601the_hungarian_agricu-91) exports related to agriculture make up 20–25% of the total. About half of Hungary's total land area is agricultural area under cultivation; this ratio is prominent among other EU members.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-6601the_hungarian_agricu-91) This is due to the country's favorable conditions including [continental climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_climate "Continental climate") and the [plains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Hungarian_Plain "Great Hungarian Plain") that make up about half of Hungary's landscape. The most important crops are wheat, corn, sunflower, potato, sugar beet, canola and a wide variety of fruits (notably apple, peach, pear, grape, watermelon, plum etc.). Hungary has [several wine regions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_wine "Hungarian wine") producing among others the worldwide famous white dessert wine [Tokaji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokaji "Tokaji") and the red [Bull's Blood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bull's_Blood "Bull's Blood"). Another traditional world-famous alcoholic drink is the fruit brandy _[pálinka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%A1linka "Pálinka")_.

Mainly cattle, pigs, poultry and sheep are raised in the country. The livestock includes the [Hungarian Grey Cattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Grey_Cattle "Hungarian Grey Cattle") which is a major tourist attraction in the [Hortobágy National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hortob%C3%A1gy_National_Park "Hortobágy National Park"). An important component of the country's gastronomic heritage is [foie gras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foie_gras "Foie gras") with about 33,000 farmers engaged in the industry. Hungary is the second largest world producer and the biggest exporter of foie gras (exporting mainly to [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France")).

Another symbol of Hungarian agriculture and cuisine is the _[paprika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paprika "Paprika")_ (both sweet and hot types). The country is one of the leading paprika producers of the world with [Szeged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szeged "Szeged") and [Kalocsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalocsa "Kalocsa") being the centres of production.

Hungary produced, in 2018, 7.9 million tons of [maize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize "Maize") (15th largest producer in the world); 5.2 million tons of [wheat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheat "Wheat"); 1.8 million tons of [sunflower seed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunflower_seed "Sunflower seed") (8th largest producer in the world); 1.1 million tons of [barley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barley "Barley"); 1 million tons of [rapeseed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapeseed "Rapeseed") (14th largest producer in the world); 941 thousand tons of [sugar beet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar_beet "Sugar beet"), which is used to produce [sugar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar "Sugar") and [ethanol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethanol "Ethanol"); 674 thousand tons of [apple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple "Apple"); 539 thousand tons of [grape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grape "Grape"); 330 thousand tons of [potato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato "Potato"); 330 thousand tons of [triticale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triticale "Triticale"); in addition to smaller productions of other agricultural products.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-97)

### Industry

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Hungary&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Industry")]

See also: [Category:Manufacturing in Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Manufacturing_in_Hungary "Category:Manufacturing in Hungary")

The main sectors of Hungarian industry are heavy industry (mining, metallurgy, machine and steel production), energy production, mechanical engineering, chemicals, food industry and automobile production. The industry is leaning mainly on processing industry and (including construction) accounted for 29.32% of GDP in 2008.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-8704elemz_i_reakci_k_az_-98) Due to the sparse energy and raw material resources, Hungary is forced to import most of these materials to satisfy the demands of the industry. Following the transition to market economy, the industry underwent restructuring and remarkable modernization. The leading industry is machinery, followed by chemical industry (plastic production, [pharmaceuticals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharmaceutical "Pharmaceutical")), while mining, [metallurgy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallurgy "Metallurgy") and textile industry seemed to be losing importance in the past two decades. In spite of the significant drop in the last decade, Hungary's food industry is still giving up to 14% of total industrial production and amounts to 7–8% of the country's exports.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-6904food_industry-99)

Nearly 50% of energy consumption is dependent on imported energy sources. Gas and oil are transported through pipelines from Russia forming 72% of the energy structure, while nuclear power produced by the [nuclear power station of Paks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paks_Nuclear_Power_Plant "Paks Nuclear Power Plant") accounts for 53,6%.

### Services

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Hungary&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Services")]

The tertiary (service) sector is the largest component of the Hungarian economy, accounting for approximately 65.5% of GDP in 2023 and employing over 63% of the workforce.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-Eurostat_sector_contribution2-111) Located in the heart of Central Europe, the country's geostrategic position has been a key factor in the growth of its service sector, attracting investment in logistics, finance, and business services.

Hungary's economy is heavily reliant on foreign trade. In 2023, the total value of goods exports was €149.2 billion, while imports stood at €139.4 billion, resulting in a trade surplus of €9.8 billion. The vast majority of this trade is with other European Union member states, with Germany being the most significant trading partner.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-KSH_trade_20232-112)

#### Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Hungary&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Education")]

Main article: [Education in Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_in_Hungary "Education in Hungary")

[![Image 58](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Language_learning_among_Hungarian_students.png/250px-Language_learning_among_Hungarian_students.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Language_learning_among_Hungarian_students.png)

Language learning among students in upper secondary education in Hungary in 2007

[Education in Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_in_Hungary "Education in Hungary") is free and compulsory from the age of 5 to 16.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-educ-113) The state provides free pre-primary schooling for all children, 8 years of general education and 4 years of upper secondary level general or vocational education.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-educ-113) Higher education system follows the three-cycle structure and the credit system of the [bologna process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bologna_process "Bologna process").[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-educ-113) Governments aim to reach European standards and encourage international mobility by putting emphasis on digital literacy, and enhancing foreign language studies: all secondary level schools teach foreign languages and at least one language certificate is needed for the acquisition of a diploma.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-educ-113) Over the past decade, this resulted in a drastic increase in the number of people speaking at least one foreign language.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-114)

Hungary's most prestigious universities are:

*   Semmelweis University with five schools (medical school, dentistry, pharmacy, nursing and physical education).
*   [Eötvös Loránd University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E%C3%B6tv%C3%B6s_Lor%C3%A1nd_University "Eötvös Loránd University") (_Eötvos Loránd Tudományegyetem_, or ELTE, which is among the top 500 universities in the world[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-115))
*   [Budapest University of Technology and Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budapest_University_of_Technology_and_Economics "Budapest University of Technology and Economics") (_Budapesti Műszaki és Gazdaságtudományi Egyetem_, or BME) BME is considered the oldest Institutes of Technology of university rank and structure in the world. Established 1782.
*   [Corvinus University of Budapest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corvinus_University_of_Budapest "Corvinus University of Budapest") (_Budapesti Corvinus Egyetem_, or BCE)
*   [Central European University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_European_University "Central European University") (_Közép-európai Egyetem_, or CEU)
*   [University of Pécs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_P%C3%A9cs "University of Pécs") (_Pécsi Tudományegyetem_, or PTE)
*   [University of Miskolc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Miskolc "University of Miskolc") (_Miskolci Egyetem_ or ME)
*   [University of Szeged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Szeged "University of Szeged") (_Szegedi Tudományegyetem_ or SZTE) In 2010, the QS World University Rankings put the University of Szeged as 451st–500th among universities globally.
*   [University of Debrecen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Debrecen "University of Debrecen") (_Debreceni Egyetem_ or DE)

Financial sources for education are mainly provided by the state (making up 5.1–5.3% of the annual GDP).[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-educ-113) In order to improve the quality of higher education, the government encourages contributions by students and companies. Another important contributor is the EU.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-educ-113)

[![Image 59](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/Pisa2006.png/250px-Pisa2006.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pisa2006.png)

Mathematics score in PISA 2006 of Hungary among other countries

The system has weaknesses, the most important being segregation and unequal access to quality education.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-educ-113) The 2006 PISA report concluded that while students from comprehensive schools did better than the OECD average, pupils from vocational secondary schools did much worse.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-eduoecd-116) Another problem is of the higher education's: response to regional and labour market needs is insufficient.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-educ-113) Government plans include improving the career guidance system and establishing a national digital network that will enable the tracking of jobs and facilitate the integration into the labour market.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-educ-113)

#### Healthcare

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Hungary&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Healthcare")]

Main article: [Healthcare in Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthcare_in_Hungary "Healthcare in Hungary")

[![Image 60](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/Total_health_expenditure_as_a_Percentage_of_GDP_%282005-2008%29.JPG/330px-Total_health_expenditure_as_a_Percentage_of_GDP_%282005-2008%29.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Total_health_expenditure_as_a_Percentage_of_GDP_(2005-2008).JPG)

Total health spending as a percentage of GDP for Hungary compared amongst various other first world nations from 2005 to 2008

Hungary has a tax-funded [universal health care](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_health_care "Universal health care") system, organized by the state-owned National Healthcare Fund ([Hungarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_language "Hungarian language"): _Országos Egészségbiztosítási Pénztár (OEP)_). Health insurance is not directly paid for by children, mothers or fathers with baby, students, [pensioners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pensioner "Pensioner"), [people with socially poor background](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poverty "Poverty"), [handicapped people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handicapped_people "Handicapped people") (including physical and mental disorders),[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-117)[priests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priest "Priest") and other church employees.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-118) Health in Hungary can be described with a rapidly growing [life expectancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_expectancy "Life expectancy") and a very low [infant mortality rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infant_mortality_rate "Infant mortality rate") (4.9 per 1,000 [live births](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_birth_(human) "Live birth (human)") in 2012).[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-KSH-119) Hungary spent 7.4% of the GDP on health care in 2009 (it was 7.0% in 2000), lower than the average of the [OECD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OECD "OECD"). Total health expenditure was 1,511 US$ per capita in 2009, 1,053 US$ governmental-fund (69.7%) and 458 US$ private-fund (30.3%)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-120) but has now risen to 2047 US$ per capita (as per 2018 data), roughly a 33% increase total, with the government funding 1439 US$ (70.3%) of the total versus the private funding 608 US$ (29.7%).[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-121) This amount totals to 6.6% of the country's total GDP, roughly a percent decrease overall.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Hungary#cite_note-122)
