years.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-25)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-26) This treasure has contributed to the understanding of social hierarchy and stratification in Europe's earliest societies.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-27)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-CENTCOM-28)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-29)

Some time before the 12th century BC, the [Thracians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thracians "Thracians"), one of the three primary ancestral groups of modern [Bulgarians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarians "Bulgarians"), appeared on the [Balkan Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balkan_Peninsula "Balkan Peninsula").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrampton19871-30)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EBBulgars-31)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-32) The Thracians were tribal and stateless, but nevertheless excelled in [metallurgy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallurgy "Metallurgy") and gave the [Greeks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greece "Ancient Greece") the [Orphean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orpheus "Orpheus") and [Dionysian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dionysus "Dionysus") cults.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EBBalkans-33) Thracian unity was catalysed by the [Persian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achaemenid_Empire "Achaemenid Empire") invasions of present-day Bulgarian territories that began in the 6th century BC.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-34) Following the defeat of the second Persian invasion in [479 BC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Persian_invasion_of_Greece "Second Persian invasion of Greece"),[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoisman2011135%E2%80%93138,_343%E2%80%93345-35) most of the Thracian tribes united under king [Teres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teres_I "Teres I") to form the [Odrysian kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odrysian_kingdom "Odrysian kingdom").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EBBalkans-33)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoisman2011135%E2%80%93138,_343%E2%80%93345-35)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-36) It was weakened and vassalised by [Philip II of Macedon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_II_of_Macedon "Philip II of Macedon") in 341 BC,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-37) attacked [by Celts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tylis "Tylis") in the 3rd century,[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-38) and finally [became a province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thracia "Thracia") of the [Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire") in AD 45.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-39)

Roman governance over the entire Balkan Peninsula was established by the end of the 1st century AD. [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") began spreading in the region around the 4th century;[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EBBalkans-33) within this current, [Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goths "Goths") bishop [Ulfilas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulfilas "Ulfilas") created the [Gothic Bible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_Bible "Gothic Bible")—the first [Germanic language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germanic_languages "Germanic languages") book—in what is today northern Bulgaria around 381.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-40) The [Byzantines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine "Byzantine") inherited the Balkan region following the [fall of Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Western_Roman_Empire "Fall of the Western Roman Empire") in 476, but their prolonged military campaigns against Persia left these territories vulnerable to barbarian incursions.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-41) This allowed the [Slavs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Slavs "Early Slavs") to enter the Balkan Peninsula and gradually turn its interior into a country of the [South Slavs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sclaveni "Sclaveni"), who lived under a [democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy "Democracy").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-42)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-43)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-44) The partially [Hellenised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellenistic_period#Balkans "Hellenistic period"), [Romanised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thraco-Romans "Thraco-Romans"), and [Gothicised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thracian_Goths "Thracian Goths") Thracians were subsequently assimilated by the newcomers.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDermott199819-45)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-46)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-47)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-48)

### First Bulgarian Empire

Main article: [First Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Bulgarian_Empire "First Bulgarian Empire")

Not long after the Slavic incursion, the region was once again invaded, this time by the [Bulgars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgars "Bulgars") under [Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khan_(title) "Khan (title)")[Asparukh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asparukh "Asparukh").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-49) Their horde was a remnant of [Old Great Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Great_Bulgaria "Old Great Bulgaria"), an extinct tribal confederacy situated north of the Black Sea in what is now Ukraine and southern [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia"). Asparukh attacked Byzantine territories in [Moesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moesia "Moesia") and conquered the Slavic tribes there in 680.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EBBulgars-31) A peace treaty with the [Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire") was signed in 681, marking the foundation of the [First Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Bulgarian_Empire "First Bulgarian Empire"). The Bulgars formed a close-knit ruling minority caste.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-fine-50)

[![Image 18: a painting depicting Bulgarian Emperor Simeon I](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/Car_Simeon_Bulharsky_-_Alfons_Mucha.jpg/250px-Car_Simeon_Bulharsky_-_Alfons_Mucha.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Car_Simeon_Bulharsky_-_Alfons_Mucha.jpg)

Emperor [Simeon I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simeon_I_of_Bulgaria "Simeon I of Bulgaria"): The Morning Star of Slavonic Literature, _[The Slav Epic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Slav\_Epic "The Slav Epic") cycle by [Alfons Mucha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfons\_Mucha "Alfons Mucha")_

Succeeding rulers strengthened the Bulgarian state throughout the 8th and 9th centuries. [Krum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krum "Krum") introduced a written code of law and checked a major Byzantine invasion at the [Battle of Pliska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Pliska "Battle of Pliska"), where Byzantine emperor [Nicephorus I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicephorus_I "Nicephorus I") was killed.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-51)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-52)[Boris I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_I_of_Bulgaria "Boris I of Bulgaria") abolished Bulgar paganism in favour of [Eastern Orthodox Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Orthodox_Church "Eastern Orthodox Church") in 864. The [conversion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianization_of_Bulgaria "Christianization of Bulgaria") was followed by a Byzantine recognition of the [Bulgarian church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_Orthodox_Church "Bulgarian Orthodox Church")[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-53) and the adoption of the [Cyrillic alphabet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrillic_script "Cyrillic script"), developed in the capital [Preslav](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preslav "Preslav").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrampton200712%E2%80%9313-54) The common language, religion and script strengthened central authority and gradually fused the Slavs and Bulgars into a unified people speaking a single [Slavic language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavic_languages "Slavic languages").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EB-55)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrampton200712%E2%80%9313-54) A [golden age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Age_of_Bulgaria "Golden Age of Bulgaria") began during the 34-year rule of [Simeon the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simeon_the_Great "Simeon the Great"), who oversaw the largest territorial expansion of the state.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_First_Golden_Age-56) Literature produced in Old Bulgarian soon spread north throughout Eastern Europe, the language itself becoming a [lingua franca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingua_franca "Lingua franca") of the region.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-ReferenceA-57)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-58)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-59)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-60)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-fortson-61) These political, cultural and religious advances turned Bulgaria into one of the [great medieval powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_medieval_great_powers "List of medieval great powers") in Europe at that time, alongside the Byzantine Empire and the [Frankish realm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolingian_Empire "Carolingian Empire").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-62)

After Simeon's death in 927, the empire was weakened by wars with [Magyars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magyars "Magyars") and [Pechenegs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pechenegs "Pechenegs") and the spread of [Bogomil heresy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bogomilism "Bogomilism").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EB-55)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-63) Simeon's successor [Peter I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_I_of_Bulgaria "Peter I of Bulgaria") faced revolts by two of his three brothers, but both were quelled.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-64) His reign stabilised the empire through a favourable [peace treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine%E2%80%93Bulgarian_Treaty_of_927 "Byzantine–Bulgarian Treaty of 927") with the Byzantines, reinforced with a marriage between Peter and Byzantine emperor [Romanos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanos_I_Lekapenos "Romanos I Lekapenos")' granddaughter.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-65)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-fine161-66)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-67)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-68) The agreement ushered in a period of 40 years of peaceful relations between the two powers and domestic prosperity.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-stephenson25-69)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-70) This lasted until 965, when war with Byzantium broke out once more; Peter suffered a stroke and retired to a monastery, dying in 969.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-71)

[Preslav](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veliki_Preslav "Veliki Preslav") was seized by the Byzantine army in 971 after consecutive [Rus'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kievan_Rus' "Kievan Rus'") and Byzantine invasions.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EB-55) The empire briefly recovered from the attacks under [Samuil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_of_Bulgaria "Samuel of Bulgaria"), but this ended when Byzantine emperor [Basil II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basil_II "Basil II") defeated the Bulgarian army at [Klyuch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Kleidion "Battle of Kleidion") in 1014.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-72) Samuil died shortly after the battle, and by 1018 the Byzantines [had conquered the First Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_conquest_of_Bulgaria "Byzantine conquest of Bulgaria").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-73)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrampton19874-74) Basil II prevented revolts by retaining the rule of local nobility, integrating them in [Byzantine bureaucracy and aristocracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_bureaucracy_and_aristocracy "Byzantine bureaucracy and aristocracy"), and relieving their lands of the obligation to pay taxes in gold, allowing [tax in kind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_in_kind "Tax in kind") instead.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Averil-75)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Ostrog-76) The [Bulgarian Patriarchate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_Orthodox_Church "Bulgarian Orthodox Church") was reduced to an [archbishopric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthodox_Archbishopric_of_Ohrid_(ancient) "Orthodox Archbishopric of Ohrid (ancient)"), but retained its [autocephalous status](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autocephaly "Autocephaly") and its [dioceses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocese "Diocese").[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Ostrog-76)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Averil-75)

### Second Bulgarian Empire

Main article: [Second Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Bulgarian_Empire "Second Bulgarian Empire")

[![Image 19: A map of the Bulgarian Empire in the mid 13th century](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/Bulgaria-Iv%C3%A1n_Asen2-es.svg/250px-Bulgaria-Iv%C3%A1n_Asen2-es.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bulgaria-Iv%C3%A1n_Asen2-es.svg)

A map showing the greatest territorial extension of the Second Bulgarian Empire during the reign of Ivan Asen II (1218–1241)

Following the death of Basil II in 1025, Byzantine domestic policy shifted from centralized, militaristic consolidation to a fragile, civilian-led administration that neglected provincial defences, directly triggering massive unrest—most notably the [uprising of Peter Delyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uprising_of_Peter_Delyan "Uprising of Peter Delyan") (1040–41)—as alienated Bulgarian subjects and disgruntled military elites rebelled against crushing taxation and bureaucratic mismanagement. The empire's authority declined after a catastrophic military [defeat at Manzikert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Manzikert "Battle of Manzikert") against [Seljuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seljuk_Empire "Seljuk Empire") invaders, and was further disturbed by the [Crusades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crusades "Crusades"). This upended Byzantine [Hellenisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellenisation "Hellenisation") attempts and created fertile ground for further revolt. [Asen dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asen_dynasty "Asen dynasty") nobles [Ivan Asen I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Asen_I "Ivan Asen I") and [Peter IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_IV_of_Bulgaria "Peter IV of Bulgaria") used the opportunity to organise a [major uprising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uprising_of_Asen_and_Peter "Uprising of Asen and Peter") and succeeded in re-establishing the Bulgarian state with a new capital in [Tarnovo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veliko_Tarnovo "Veliko Tarnovo").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EBSecondEmpire-77)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-78)

[Kaloyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaloyan "Kaloyan"), the third of the Asen monarchs, extended his dominion to [Belgrade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgrade "Belgrade") and [Ohrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohrid "Ohrid"). He acknowledged the spiritual supremacy of [the pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_pope "The pope") and received a royal crown from a [papal legate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papal_legate "Papal legate").[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EB1911-79)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-80) The empire reached its zenith under [Ivan Asen II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Asen_II "Ivan Asen II") (1218–1241), when its borders expanded as far as the coast of [Albania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albania "Albania"), Serbia and [Epirus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epirus "Epirus"), while commerce and culture flourished.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EB1911-79)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EBSecondEmpire-77) Ivan Asen's rule was also marked by a shift away from Rome in religious matters.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrampton19876-81)

The Asen dynasty became extinct in 1257. Internal strife and incessant Byzantine, Hungarian and Mongol attacks followed, allowing the [Golden Horde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Horde "Golden Horde") to [establish suzerainty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_invasion_of_Bulgaria_and_Serbia "Mongol invasion of Bulgaria and Serbia") over the weakened Bulgarian state.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EB1911-79)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrampton19876-81) The Mongols were expelled by swineherd [Ivaylo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivaylo_of_Bulgaria "Ivaylo of Bulgaria"), who led a [great peasant revolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uprising_of_Ivaylo "Uprising of Ivaylo") that briefly made him emperor in 1277.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Martin_2017-82)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EBSecondEmpire-77) His short-lived reign ended in 1280 when he was overthrown by [the feudal landlords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyars "Boyars"),[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Martin_2017-82) whose subsequent factional conflicts caused the Second Bulgarian Empire to disintegrate into small feudal dominions by the 14th century.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EBSecondEmpire-77) Despite a brief resurgence in the arts and culture,[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-f436-83)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-k337-84)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-85) the remaining Bulgarian [rump states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rump_state "Rump state")—two tsardoms at [Vidin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsardom_of_Vidin "Tsardom of Vidin") and [Tarnovo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Bulgarian_Empire#Ivan_Alexander_and_fall_of_Bulgaria "Second Bulgarian Empire") and the [Despotate of Dobrudzha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Despotate_of_Dobruja "Despotate of Dobruja")—became easy prey for a new threat arriving from the Southeast: the [Ottoman Turks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Turks "Ottoman Turks").[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EB1911-79)

### Ottoman rule

Main article: [Ottoman Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Bulgaria "Ottoman Bulgaria")

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Battle_of_Nicopolis.jpg/250px-Battle_of_Nicopolis.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Battle_of_Nicopolis.jpg)

The Battle of Nicopolis in 1396 marked the end of medieval Bulgarian statehood.

The Ottomans were employed as mercenaries by the Byzantines in the 1340s, but later became invaders in their own right.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Ottoman_rule-86) Sultan [Murad I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murad_I "Murad I") took [Adrianople](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrianople "Adrianople") from the Byzantines in 1362; [Sofia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia "Sofia") fell in 1382, followed by [Shumen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shumen "Shumen") in 1388.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Ottoman_rule-86) The Ottomans completed their conquest of Bulgarian lands in 1393 when Tarnovo was sacked after a three-month siege and the [Battle of Nicopolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Nicopolis "Battle of Nicopolis") which brought about the fall of the [Vidin Tsardom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsardom_of_Vidin "Tsardom of Vidin") in 1396. [Sozopol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sozopol "Sozopol") was the last Bulgarian settlement to fall, in 1453.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-87) The Bulgarian nobility was subsequently eliminated and the peasantry was [enserfed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serfdom "Serfdom") to Ottoman masters,[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Ottoman_rule-86) while much of the educated clergy fled to other countries.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Jire%C4%8Dek-88)

Bulgarians were subjected to heavy taxes (including [Devshirme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devshirme "Devshirme"), or _blood tax_), their culture was suppressed,[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Jire%C4%8Dek-88) and they experienced partial [Islamisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamisation "Islamisation").[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-89) Ottoman authorities established a religious administrative community called the [Rum Millet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rum_Millet "Rum Millet"), which governed all Orthodox Christians regardless of their ethnicity.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-90) Most of the local population then gradually lost its distinct national consciousness, identifying only by its faith.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-91)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-92) The clergy remaining in some isolated monasteries kept their ethnic identity alive, enabling its survival in remote rural areas,[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrampton19878-93) and in the militant [Catholic community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church_in_Bulgaria "Catholic Church in Bulgaria") in the northwest of the country.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-94)

As Ottoman power began to wane, [Habsburg Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habsburg_monarchy "Habsburg monarchy") and Russia saw Bulgarian Christians as potential allies. The Austrians first backed an [uprising in Tarnovo in 1598](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Tarnovo_Uprising "First Tarnovo Uprising"), then [a second one in 1686](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Tarnovo_Uprising "Second Tarnovo Uprising"), the [Chiprovtsi Uprising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiprovtsi_Uprising "Chiprovtsi Uprising") in 1688 and finally [Karposh's rebellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karposh's_rebellion "Karposh's rebellion") in 1689.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Decline-95) The [Russian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Empire "Russian Empire") also asserted itself as a protector of Christians in Ottoman lands with the [Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_K%C3%BC%C3%A7%C3%BCk_Kaynarca "Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca") in 1774.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Decline-95)

[![Image 21: The Defence of the Eagle's Nest, painting by Alexey Popov from 1893, depicting the Defence of Shipka Pass](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/The_defeat_of_Shipka_Peak%2C_Bulgarian_War_of_Independence.JPG/250px-The_defeat_of_Shipka_Peak%2C_Bulgarian_War_of_Independence.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_defeat_of_Shipka_Peak,_Bulgarian_War_of_Independence.JPG)

The Russo-Bulgarian defence of Shipka Pass in 1877

The Western European [Enlightenment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment "Age of Enlightenment") in the 18th century influenced the initiation of a [national awakening of Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_awakening_of_Bulgaria "National awakening of Bulgaria").[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Ottoman_rule-86) It restored national consciousness and provided an ideological basis for the liberation struggle, resulting in the [April Uprising of 1876](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_Uprising_of_1876 "April Uprising of 1876"). Up to 30,000 Bulgarians were killed as Ottoman authorities put down the rebellion. The massacres prompted the [Great Powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Powers#History "Great Powers") to take action.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_Final_Move_to_Independence-96) They convened the [Constantinople Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantinople_Conference "Constantinople Conference") in 1876, but their decisions were rejected by the Ottomans. This allowed the Russian Empire to seek a military solution without risking confrontation with other Great Powers, as had happened in the [Crimean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimean_War "Crimean War").[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_Final_Move_to_Independence-96) In 1877, [Russia declared war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Turkish_War_(1877%E2%80%931878) "Russo-Turkish War (1877–1878)") on the Ottomans and defeated them with the help of [Bulgarian rebels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opalchentsi "Opalchentsi"), particularly during the crucial [Battle of Shipka Pass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Shipka_Pass "Battle of Shipka Pass") which secured Russian control over the main road to [Constantinople](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantinople "Constantinople").[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-97)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-98)

### Third Bulgarian state

Main articles: [History of Bulgaria (1878–1946)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Bulgaria_(1878%E2%80%931946) "History of Bulgaria (1878–1946)"), [People's Republic of Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_Bulgaria "People's Republic of Bulgaria"), and [History of Bulgaria since 1989](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Bulgaria_since_1989 "History of Bulgaria since 1989")

[![Image 22: Map of Bulgaria according to the Treaty of San Stefano](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/Bulgaria-SanStefano_-%281878%29-byTodorBozhinov.png/330px-Bulgaria-SanStefano_-%281878%29-byTodorBozhinov.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bulgaria-SanStefano_-(1878)-byTodorBozhinov.png)

Borders of Bulgaria according to the preliminary Treaty of San Stefano

The [Treaty of San Stefano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_San_Stefano "Treaty of San Stefano") was signed on 3 March 1878 by [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Empire "Russian Empire") and the [Ottoman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire"). It was to set up an autonomous Bulgarian principality spanning [Moesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moesia "Moesia"), [Macedonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macedonia_(region) "Macedonia (region)") and [Thrace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrace "Thrace"), roughly on the territories of the [Second Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Bulgarian_Empire "Second Bulgarian Empire"),[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTESan_Stefano,_Berlin_and_Independence-99)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-100) and this day is now [a public holiday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_holidays_in_Bulgaria "Public holidays in Bulgaria") called [National Liberation Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberation_Day_(Bulgaria) "Liberation Day (Bulgaria)").[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-101) The other [Great Powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Powers#History "Great Powers") immediately rejected the treaty out of fear that such a large country in the [Balkans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balkans "Balkans") might threaten their interests. It was superseded by the [Treaty of Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Berlin,_1878 "Treaty of Berlin, 1878"), signed on 13 July. It provided for a much smaller state, the [Principality of Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principality_of_Bulgaria "Principality of Bulgaria"), only comprising Moesia and the region of [Sofia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia "Sofia"), and leaving large populations of ethnic Bulgarians outside the new country.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTESan_Stefano,_Berlin_and_Independence-99)[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-BBCProfile-102) This significantly contributed to Bulgaria's militaristic foreign affairs approach during the first half of the 20th century.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHistorical_Setting-103)

The Bulgarian principality won [a war against Serbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbo-Bulgarian_War "Serbo-Bulgarian War") and incorporated the semi-autonomous Ottoman territory of [Eastern Rumelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Rumelia "Eastern Rumelia") in 1885, proclaiming itself the independent Kingdom of Bulgaria on 5 October 1908.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrampton2007174-104) In the years following independence, Bulgaria increasingly militarised and was often referred to as "the Balkan [Prussia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prussia "Prussia")".[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-105) It became involved in three consecutive conflicts between 1912 and 1918—two [Balkan Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balkan_Wars "Balkan Wars") and [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"). After a disastrous defeat in the [Second Balkan War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Balkan_War "Second Balkan War"), Bulgaria again found itself fighting on the losing side as a result of its alliance with the [Central Powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Powers "Central Powers") in World War I. Despite fielding more than a quarter of its population in a 1,200,000-strong army[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-106)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-107) and achieving several decisive victories at [Doiran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Doiran_(1917) "Battle of Doiran (1917)") and [Monastir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Monastir_(1917) "Battle of Monastir (1917)"), the country capitulated in 1918. The war resulted in significant territorial losses and a total of 87,500 soldiers killed.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-108) More than 253,000 refugees from the lost territories [immigrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immigration "Immigration") to Bulgaria from 1912 to 1929,[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-109) placing additional strain on the already ruined national economy.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-110)

[![Image 23: A portrait of Tsar Boris III](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/BASA-3K-7-342-28-Boris_III_of_Bulgaria.jpeg/250px-BASA-3K-7-342-28-Boris_III_of_Bulgaria.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BASA-3K-7-342-28-Boris_III_of_Bulgaria.jpeg)

Tsar Boris III

The resulting political unrest led to the establishment of a royal [authoritarian dictatorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authoritarianism "Authoritarianism") by Tsar [Boris III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_III_of_Bulgaria "Boris III of Bulgaria") (1918–1943). Bulgaria entered World War II in 1941 as a member of [the Axis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axis_powers "Axis powers") but declined to participate in [Operation Barbarossa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Barbarossa "Operation Barbarossa") and [saved its Jewish population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rescue_of_the_Bulgarian_Jews "Rescue of the Bulgarian Jews") from deportation to [concentration camps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_concentration_camps "Nazi concentration camps").[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBulgaria_in_World_War_II:_The_Passive_Alliance-111) The sudden death of Boris III in mid-1943 pushed the country into political turmoil as the war turned against Germany, and the communist guerrilla movement gained momentum. The government of [Bogdan Filov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bogdan_Filov "Bogdan Filov") subsequently failed to achieve peace with the Allies. Bulgaria did not comply with Soviet demands to expel German forces from its territory, resulting in a declaration of war and an invasion by the USSR in September 1944.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWartime_Crisis-112) The communist-dominated [Fatherland Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatherland_Front_(Bulgaria) "Fatherland Front (Bulgaria)") took power, ended participation in the Axis and joined the Allied side until the war ended.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-113) Bulgaria suffered little war damage and the Soviet Union demanded no reparations. But all wartime territorial gains, with the notable exception of [Southern Dobrudzha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Craiova "Treaty of Craiova"), were lost.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_Soviet_Occupation-114)

[![Image 24](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4d/Georgi_Dimitrov.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Georgi_Dimitrov.jpg)

[Georgi Dimitrov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgi_Dimitrov "Georgi Dimitrov"), leader of the [Bulgarian Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_Communist_Party "Bulgarian Communist Party") from 1946 to 1949

The [left-wing coup d'état](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1944_Bulgarian_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "1944 Bulgarian coup d'état") of 9 September 1944 led to the abolition of the monarchy and [the executions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Court_(Bulgaria) "People's Court (Bulgaria)") of some 1,000–3,000 dissidents, war criminals, and members of the former royal elite.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-115)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-116)[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-117) But it was not until 1946 that a [one-party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-party_state "One-party state")[people's republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_republic "People's republic") was instituted following a referendum.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrampton2005271-118) It fell into the Soviet sphere of influence under the leadership of [Georgi Dimitrov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgi_Dimitrov "Georgi Dimitrov") (1946–1949), who established a repressive, rapidly industrialising [Stalinist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stalinist "Stalinist") state.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_Soviet_Occupation-114) By the mid-1950s, standards of living rose significantly and political repression eased.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDomestic_Policy_and_Its_Results-119)[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAfter_Stalin-120) The Soviet-style [planned economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_economy "Planned economy") saw some experimental market-oriented policies emerging under [Todor Zhivkov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Todor_Zhivkov "Todor Zhivkov") (1954–1989).[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_Economy-121) Compared to wartime levels, national [GDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_domestic_product "Gross domestic product") increased five-fold and per capita GDP quadrupled by the 1980s,[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-122) although severe debt spikes took place in 1960, 1977 and 1980.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-123) Zhivkov's daughter [Lyudmila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyudmila_Zhivkova "Lyudmila Zhivkova") bolstered national pride by promoting Bulgarian heritage, culture and arts worldwide.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_Political_Atmosphere_in_the_1970s-124) Facing declining birth rates among the ethnic Bulgarian majority, Zhivkov's government in 1984 forced the minority ethnic [Turks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_Turks "Bulgarian Turks") to adopt Slavic names in an attempt to erase their identity and assimilate them.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBulgaria_in_the_1980s-125) These policies resulted in the emigration of some 300,000 ethnic Turks to Turkey.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-126)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-127)

The Communist Party was forced to give up its political monopoly on 10 November 1989 under the influence of the [Revolutions of 1989](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutions_of_1989 "Revolutions of 1989"). Zhivkov resigned and Bulgaria embarked on a transition to a [parliamentary democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_system "Parliamentary system").[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGovernment_and_Politics-128) The first free elections in June 1990 were won by the Communist Party, now rebranded as the [Bulgarian Socialist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_Socialist_Party "Bulgarian Socialist Party").[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-129) A [new constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Bulgaria "Constitution of Bulgaria") that provided for a relatively weak elected president and for a prime minister accountable to the legislature was adopted in July 1991.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-130) The new system initially failed to improve living standards or create economic growth—the average quality of life and economic performance remained lower than under communism well into the early 2000s.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-131) After 2001, economic, political and geopolitical conditions improved greatly,[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTELibrary_of_Congress200616-132) and Bulgaria achieved high Human Development status in 2003.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-133) It became a member of [NATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO "NATO") in 2004[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-nato-134) and participated in the [War in Afghanistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_in_Afghanistan_(2001%E2%80%932021) "War in Afghanistan (2001–2021)"). After several years of reforms, it joined the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") and the [single market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Single_Market "European Single Market") in 2007, despite EU concerns over government corruption.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Ind-135) Bulgaria hosted the 2018 [Presidency of the Council of the European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_the_Council_of_the_European_Union "Presidency of the Council of the European Union") at the [National Palace of Culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Palace_of_Culture "National Palace of Culture") in [Sofia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia "Sofia").[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-136)

## Geography

Main article: [Geography of Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Bulgaria "Geography of Bulgaria")

Bulgaria is a middle-sized country situated in Southeast Europe, in the east of the Balkans. Its territory covers an area of 110,994 square kilometres (42,855 sq mi), while land borders with its five neighbouring countries run a total length of 1,808 kilometres (1,123 mi), and its coastline is 354 kilometres (220 mi) long.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTELibrary_of_Congress20064-137) Bulgaria's geographic coordinates are [43° N](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/43rd_parallel_north "43rd parallel north")[25° E](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/25th_meridian_east "25th meridian east").[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-CIA_World_Factbook-138) The most notable [topographical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topographical "Topographical") features of the country are the [Danubian Plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danubian_Plain_(Bulgaria) "Danubian Plain (Bulgaria)"), the [Balkan Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balkan_Mountains "Balkan Mountains"), the [Upper Thracian Plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Thracian_Plain "Upper Thracian Plain"), and the [Rila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rila "Rila")-[Rhodope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodope_Mountains "Rhodope Mountains")[massif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massif "Massif").[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTELibrary_of_Congress20064-137) The southern edge of the Danubian Plain slopes upward into the foothills of the Balkans, while the [Danube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danube "Danube") defines the border with Romania. The [Thracian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thracia "Thracia") Plain is roughly triangular, beginning southeast of [Sofia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia "Sofia") and broadening as it reaches the [Black Sea coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_Black_Sea_Coast "Bulgarian Black Sea Coast").[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTELibrary_of_Congress20064-137)

The Balkan mountains run laterally through the middle of the country from west to east. **Bulgaria**,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-11) officially the **Republic of Bulgaria**,[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-12) is a country in [Southeastern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Europe "Southeastern Europe"). It is situated on the eastern portion of the [Balkans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balkans "Balkans") directly south of the [Danube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danube "Danube") river and west of the [Black Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Sea "Black Sea"). Bulgaria is bordered by [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece "Greece") and [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey") to the south, [Serbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbia "Serbia") and [North Macedonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Macedonia "North Macedonia") to the west, and [Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romania "Romania") across the Danube river to the north. It covers a territory of 110,994 square kilometres (42,855 sq mi), making it the tenth largest within the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") and the [sixteenth-largest country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_European_countries_by_area "List of European countries by area") in Europe by area. [Sofia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia "Sofia") is the nation's capital and [largest city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_and_towns_in_Bulgaria "List of cities and towns in Bulgaria"); other major cities include [Plovdiv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv "Plovdiv"), [Varna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria "Varna, Bulgaria"), and [Burgas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas "Burgas").

One of the earliest societies in the lands of modern-day Bulgaria was the [Karanovo culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karanovo_culture "Karanovo culture") (6,500 BC). In the 6th to 3rd century BC, the region was a battleground for ancient [Thracians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thracians "Thracians"), [Persians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persians "Persians"), [Celts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celts "Celts"), and [Macedonians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Macedonians "Ancient Macedonians"); stability came when the [Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire") conquered the region in AD 45. After the Roman state splintered, tribal invasions in the region resumed. Around the 6th century, these territories were settled by the [early Slavs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Slavs "Early Slavs"). The [Bulgars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgars "Bulgars"), led by [Asparuh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asparuh_of_Bulgaria "Asparuh of Bulgaria"), attacked from the lands of [Old Great Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Great_Bulgaria "Old Great Bulgaria") and then permanently invaded the Balkans in the late 7th century. They established the [First Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Bulgarian_Empire "First Bulgarian Empire"), recognised by treaty in 681 AD by the [Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire"). It dominated most of the Balkans and significantly influenced [Slavic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavs "Slavs") cultures by developing the [Cyrillic script](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrillic_script "Cyrillic script"). The First Bulgarian Empire lasted until the early 11th century, when Byzantine emperor [Basil II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basil_II "Basil II") conquered and dismantled it. A [successful Bulgarian revolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uprising_of_Asen_and_Peter "Uprising of Asen and Peter") in 1185 established a [Second Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Bulgarian_Empire "Second Bulgarian Empire"), which reached its apex under [Ivan Asen II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Asen_II_of_Bulgaria "Ivan Asen II of Bulgaria") (1218–1241). After numerous exhausting wars and feudal strife, the empire disintegrated and in 1396 fell under [Ottoman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire") rule for nearly five centuries.

The [Russo-Turkish War of 1877–78](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Turkish_War_of_1877%E2%80%9378 "Russo-Turkish War of 1877–78") resulted in the formation of the third and current Bulgarian state, which declared independence from the Ottoman Empire in 1908. Many ethnic Bulgarians were left outside the new nation's borders, which stoked [irredentist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irredentist "Irredentist") sentiments that led to several conflicts with its neighbours and alliances with [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany") in both world wars. In 1946, Bulgaria came under the Soviet-led [Eastern Bloc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Bloc "Eastern Bloc") and became [a socialist state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_Bulgaria "People's Republic of Bulgaria"). The ruling [Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_Communist_Party "Bulgarian Communist Party") gave up its monopoly on power after the [revolutions of 1989](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutions_of_1989 "Revolutions of 1989") and allowed [multiparty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-party_system "Multi-party system") elections. Bulgaria then transitioned into a [democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy "Democracy").

Since adopting [a democratic constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Bulgaria "Constitution of Bulgaria") in 1991, Bulgaria has been a [parliamentary republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_republic "Parliamentary republic") composed of 28 [provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provinces_of_Bulgaria "Provinces of Bulgaria"), with a high degree of [political, administrative, and economic centralisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Bulgaria "Government of Bulgaria"). A [developed country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Developed_country "Developed country"), its [advanced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_economy "Advanced economy"), [high-income economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-income_economy "High-income economy") is part of the [European single market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_single_market "European single market") and is largely based on services, followed by [manufacturing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industry_of_Bulgaria "Industry of Bulgaria"), [mining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mining_in_Bulgaria "Mining in Bulgaria"), and [agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agriculture_in_Bulgaria "Agriculture in Bulgaria"). Bulgaria has been influenced by its role as a transit country for [natural gas and oil pipelines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_in_Bulgaria "Energy in Bulgaria"), as well as its strategic [location on the Black Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_Black_Sea_Coast "Bulgarian Black Sea Coast"). Bulgaria is a member state of the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_enlargement_of_the_European_Union "2007 enlargement of the European Union"), including the [Schengen Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schengen_Area "Schengen Area") and the [eurozone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurozone "Eurozone"), [NATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enlargement_of_NATO#Vilnius_Group "Enlargement of NATO"), and various regional suborganizations such as the [Bucharest Nine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bucharest_Nine "Bucharest Nine").

## Etymology

The name _Bulgaria_ is derived from the _[Bulgars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgars "Bulgars")_, a tribe of [Turkic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkic_peoples "Turkic peoples") origin that founded the First Bulgarian Empire. Their name is not completely understood and is difficult to trace it back earlier than the 4th century AD;[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGolden1992103%E2%80%93104-13) however, it is possibly derived from the [Proto-Turkic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Turkic "Proto-Turkic") word _bulģha_ ("to mix", "shake", "stir") and its derivative _bulgak_ ("revolt", "disorder").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-14) The meaning may be further extended to "rebel", "incite" or "produce a state of disorder", and so, in the derivative, the "disturbers".[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChen201297-15)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-16)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGolden1992104-17) Tribal groups in [Inner Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_Asia "Inner Asia") with phonologically close names were frequently described in similar terms, as the [Buluoji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jie_people "Jie people"), a component of the "[Five Barbarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Barbarians "Five Barbarians")" groups, which during the 4th century were portrayed as both: a "mixed race" and "troublemakers".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChen201292%E2%80%9395,_97-18)

### First Bulgarian Empire

Main article: [First Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Bulgarian_Empire "First Bulgarian Empire")

Not long after the Slavic incursion, the region was once again invaded, this time by the [Bulgars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgars "Bulgars") under [Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khan_(title) "Khan (title)")[Asparukh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asparukh "Asparukh").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-49) Their horde was a remnant of [Old Great Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Great_Bulgaria "Old Great Bulgaria"), an extinct tribal confederacy situated north of the Black Sea in what is now Ukraine and southern [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia"). Asparukh attacked Byzantine territories in [Moesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moesia "Moesia") and conquered the Slavic tribes there in 680.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EBBulgars-31) A peace treaty with the [Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire") was signed in 681, marking the foundation of the [First Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Bulgarian_Empire "First Bulgarian Empire"). The Bulgars formed a close-knit ruling minority caste.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-fine-50)

Slavs and Bulgars into a unified people speaking a single [Slavic language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavic_languages "Slavic languages").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EB-55)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrampton200712%E2%80%9313-54) A [golden age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Age_of_Bulgaria "Golden Age of Bulgaria") began during the 34-year rule of [Simeon the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simeon_the_Great "Simeon the Great"), who oversaw the largest territorial expansion of the state.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_First_Golden_Age-56) Literature produced in Old Bulgarian soon spread north throughout Eastern Europe, the language itself becoming a [lingua franca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingua_franca "Lingua franca") of the region.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-ReferenceA-57)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-58)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-59)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-60)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-fortson-61) These political, cultural and religious advances turned Bulgaria into one of the [great medieval powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_medieval_great_powers "List of medieval great powers") in Europe at that time, alongside the Byzantine Empire and the [Frankish realm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolingian_Empire "Carolingian Empire").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-62)

After Simeon's death in 927, the empire was weakened by wars with [Magyars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magyars "Magyars") and [Pechenegs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pechenegs "Pechenegs") and the spread of [Bogomil heresy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bogomilism "Bogomilism").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EB-55)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-63) Simeon's successor [Peter I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_I_of_Bulgaria "Peter I of Bulgaria") faced revolts by two of his three brothers, but both were quelled.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-64) His reign stabilised the empire through a favourable [peace treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine%E2%80%93Bulgarian_Treaty_of_927 "Byzantine–Bulgarian Treaty of 927") with the Byzantines, reinforced with a marriage between Peter and Byzantine emperor [Romanos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanos_I_Lekapenos "Romanos I Lekapenos")' granddaughter.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-65)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-fine161-66)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-67)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-68) The agreement ushered in a period of 40 years of peaceful relations between the two powers and domestic prosperity.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-stephenson25-69)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-70) This lasted until 965, when war with Byzantium broke out once more; Peter suffered a stroke and retired to a monastery, dying in 969.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-71)

[Preslav](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veliki_Preslav "Veliki Preslav") was seized by the Byzantine army in 971 after consecutive [Rus'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kievan_Rus' "Kievan Rus'") and Byzantine invasions.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EB-55) The empire briefly recovered from the attacks under [Samuil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_of_Bulgaria "Samuel of Bulgaria"), but this ended when Byzantine emperor [Basil II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basil_II "Basil II") defeated the Bulgarian army at [Klyuch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Kleidion "Battle of Kleidion") in 1014.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-72) Samuil died shortly after the battle, and by 1018 the Byzantines [had conquered the First Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_conquest_of_Bulgaria "Byzantine conquest of Bulgaria").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-73)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrampton19874-74) Basil II prevented revolts by retaining the rule of local nobility, integrating them in [Byzantine bureaucracy and aristocracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_bureaucracy_and_aristocracy "Byzantine bureaucracy and aristocracy"), and relieving their lands of the obligation to pay taxes in gold, allowing [tax in kind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_in_kind "Tax in kind") instead.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Averil-75)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Ostrog-76) The [Bulgarian Patriarchate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_Orthodox_Church "Bulgarian Orthodox Church") was reduced to an [archbishopric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthodox_Archbishopric_of_Ohrid_(ancient) "Orthodox Archbishopric of Ohrid (ancient)"), but retained its [autocephalous status](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autocephaly "Autocephaly") and its [dioceses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocese "Diocese").[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Ostrog-76)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Averil-75)

### Second Bulgarian Empire

Main article: [Second Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Bulgarian_Empire "Second Bulgarian Empire")

[![Image 19: A map of the Bulgarian Empire in the mid 13th century](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/Bulgaria-Iv%C3%A1n_Asen2-es.svg/250px-Bulgaria-Iv%C3%A1n_Asen2-es.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bulgaria-Iv%C3%A1n_Asen2-es.svg)

A map showing the greatest territorial extension of the Second Bulgarian Empire during the reign of Ivan Asen II (1218–1241)

Following the death of Basil II in 1025, Byzantine domestic policy shifted from centralized, militaristic consolidation to a fragile, civilian-led administration that neglected provincial defences, directly triggering massive unrest—most notably the [uprising of Peter Delyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uprising_of_Peter_Delyan "Uprising of Peter Delyan") (1040–41)—as alienated Bulgarian subjects and disgruntled military elites rebelled against crushing taxation and bureaucratic mismanagement. The empire's authority declined after a catastrophic military [defeat at Manzikert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Manzikert "Battle of Manzikert") against [Seljuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seljuk_Empire "Seljuk Empire") invaders, and was further disturbed by the [Crusades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crusades "Crusades"). This upended Byzantine [Hellenisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellenisation "Hellenisation") attempts and created fertile ground for further revolt. [Asen dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asen_dynasty "Asen dynasty") nobles [Ivan Asen I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Asen_I "Ivan Asen I") and [Peter IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_IV_of_Bulgaria "Peter IV of Bulgaria") used the opportunity to organise a [major uprising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uprising_of_Asen_and_Peter "Uprising of Asen and Peter") and succeeded in re-establishing the Bulgarian state with a new capital in [Tarnovo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veliko_Tarnovo "Veliko Tarnovo").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EBSecondEmpire-77)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-78)

[Kaloyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaloyan "Kaloyan"), the third of the Asen monarchs, extended his dominion to [Belgrade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgrade "Belgrade") and [Ohrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohrid "Ohrid"). He acknowledged the spiritual supremacy of [the pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_pope "The pope") and received a royal crown from a [papal legate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papal_legate "Papal legate").[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EB1911-79)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-80) The empire reached its zenith under [Ivan Asen II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Asen_II "Ivan Asen II") (1218–1241), when its borders expanded as far as the coast of [Albania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albania "Albania"), Serbia and [Epirus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epirus "Epirus"), while commerce and culture flourished.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EB1911-79)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EBSecondEmpire-77) Ivan Asen's rule was also marked by a shift away from Rome in religious matters.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrampton19876-81)

The Asen dynasty became extinct in 1257. Internal strife and incessant Byzantine, Hungarian and Mongol attacks followed, allowing the [Golden Horde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Horde "Golden Horde") to [establish suzerainty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_invasion_of_Bulgaria_and_Serbia "Mongol invasion of Bulgaria and Serbia") over the weakened Bulgarian state.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EB1911-79)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrampton19876-81) The Mongols were expelled by swineherd [Ivaylo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivaylo_of_Bulgaria "Ivaylo of Bulgaria"), who led a [great peasant revolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uprising_of_Ivaylo "Uprising of Ivaylo") that briefly made him emperor in 1277.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Martin_2017-82)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EBSecondEmpire-77) His short-lived reign ended in 1280 when he was overthrown by [the feudal landlords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyars "Boyars"),[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Martin_2017-82) whose subsequent factional conflicts caused the Second Bulgarian Empire to disintegrate into small feudal dominions by the 14th century.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EBSecondEmpire-77) Despite a brief resurgence in the arts and culture,[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-f436-83)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-k337-84)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-85) the remaining Bulgarian [rump states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rump_state "Rump state")—two tsardoms at [Vidin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsardom_of_Vidin "Tsardom of Vidin") and [Tarnovo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Bulgarian_Empire#Ivan_Alexander_and_fall_of_Bulgaria "Second Bulgarian Empire") and the [Despotate of Dobrudzha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Despotate_of_Dobruja "Despotate of Dobruja")—became easy prey for a new threat arriving from the Southeast: the [Ottoman Turks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Turks "Ottoman Turks").[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-EB1911-79)

### Ottoman rule

Main article: [Ottoman Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Bulgaria "Ottoman Bulgaria")

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Battle_of_Nicopolis.jpg/250px-Battle_of_Nicopolis.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Battle_of_Nicopolis.jpg)

The Battle of Nicopolis in 1396 marked the end of medieval Bulgarian statehood.

The Ottomans were employed as mercenaries by the Byzantines in the 1340s, but later became invaders in their own right.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Ottoman_rule-86) Sultan [Murad I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murad_I "Murad I") took [Adrianople](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrianople "Adrianople") from the Byzantines in 1362; [Sofia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia "Sofia") fell in 1382, followed by [Shumen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shumen "Shumen") in 1388.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Ottoman_rule-86) The Ottomans completed their conquest of Bulgarian lands in 1393 when Tarnovo was sacked after a three-month siege and the [Battle of Nicopolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Nicopolis "Battle of Nicopolis") which brought about the fall of the [Vidin Tsardom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsardom_of_Vidin "Tsardom of Vidin") in 1396. [Sozopol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sozopol "Sozopol") was the last Bulgarian settlement to fall, in 1453.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-87) The Bulgarian nobility was subsequently eliminated and the peasantry was [enserfed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serfdom "Serfdom") to Ottoman masters,[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Ottoman_rule-86) while much of the educated clergy fled to other countries.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Jire%C4%8Dek-88)

Bulgarians were subjected to heavy taxes (including [Devshirme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devshirme "Devshirme"), or _blood tax_), their culture was suppressed,[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Jire%C4%8Dek-88) and they experienced partial [Islamisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamisation "Islamisation").[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-89) Ottoman authorities established a religious administrative community called the [Rum Millet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rum_Millet "Rum Millet"), which governed all Orthodox Christians regardless of their ethnicity.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-90) Most of the local population then gradually lost its distinct national consciousness, identifying only by its faith.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-91)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-92) The clergy remaining in some isolated monasteries kept their ethnic identity alive, enabling its survival in remote rural areas,[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrampton19878-93) and in the militant [Catholic community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church_in_Bulgaria "Catholic Church in Bulgaria") in the northwest of the country.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-94)

As Ottoman power began to wane, [Habsburg Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habsburg_monarchy "Habsburg monarchy") and Russia saw Bulgarian Christians as potential allies. The Austrians first backed an [uprising in Tarnovo in 1598](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Tarnovo_Uprising "First Tarnovo Uprising"), then [a second one in 1686](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Tarnovo_Uprising "Second Tarnovo Uprising"), the [Chiprovtsi Uprising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiprovtsi_Uprising "Chiprovtsi Uprising") in 1688 and finally [Karposh's rebellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karposh's_rebellion "Karposh's rebellion") in 1689.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Decline-95) The [Russian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Empire "Russian Empire") also asserted itself as a protector of Christians in Ottoman lands with the [Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_K%C3%BC%C3%A7%C3%BCk_Kaynarca "Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca") in 1774.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Decline-95)

[![Image 21: The Defence of the Eagle's Nest, painting by Alexey Popov from 1893, depicting the Defence of Shipka Pass](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/The_defeat_of_Shipka_Peak%2C_Bulgarian_War_of_Independence.JPG/250px-The_defeat_of_Shipka_Peak%2C_Bulgarian_War_of_Independence.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_defeat_of_Shipka_Peak,_Bulgarian_War_of_Independence.JPG)

The Russo-Bulgarian defence of Shipka Pass in 1877

The Western European [Enlightenment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment "Age of Enlightenment") in the 18th century influenced the initiation of a [national awakening of Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_awakening_of_Bulgaria "National awakening of Bulgaria").[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-Ottoman_rule-86) It restored national consciousness and provided an ideological basis for the liberation struggle, resulting in the [April Uprising of 1876](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_Uprising_of_1876 "April Uprising of 1876"). Up to 30,000 Bulgarians were killed as Ottoman authorities put down the rebellion. The massacres prompted the [Great Powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Powers#History "Great Powers") to take action.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_Final_Move_to_Independence-96) They convened the [Constantinople Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantinople_Conference "Constantinople Conference") in 1876, but their decisions were rejected by the Ottomans. This allowed the Russian Empire to seek a military solution without risking confrontation with other Great Powers, as had happened in the [Crimean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimean_War "Crimean War").[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_Final_Move_to_Independence-96) In 1877, [Russia declared war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Turkish_War_(1877%E2%80%931878) "Russo-Turkish War (1877–1878)") on the Ottomans and defeated them with the help of [Bulgarian rebels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opalchentsi "Opalchentsi"), particularly during the crucial [Battle of Shipka Pass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Shipka_Pass "Battle of Shipka Pass") which secured Russian control over the main road to [Constantinople](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantinople "Constantinople").[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-97)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-98)

### Third Bulgarian state

Main articles: [History of Bulgaria (1878–1946)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Bulgaria_(1878%E2%80%931946) "History of Bulgaria (1878–1946)"), [People's Republic of Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_Bulgaria "People's Republic of Bulgaria"), and [History of Bulgaria since 1989](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Bulgaria_since_1989 "History of Bulgaria since 1989")

[![Image 22: Map of Bulgaria according to the Treaty of San Stefano](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/Bulgaria-SanStefano_-%281878%29-byTodorBozhinov.png/330px-Bulgaria-SanStefano_-%281878%29-byTodorBozhinov.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bulgaria-SanStefano_-(1878)-byTodorBozhinov.png)

Borders of Bulgaria according to the preliminary Treaty of San Stefano

The [Treaty of San Stefano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_San_Stefano "Treaty of San Stefano") was signed on 3 March 1878 by [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Empire "Russian Empire") and the [Ottoman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire"). It was to set up an autonomous Bulgarian principality spanning [Moesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moesia "Moesia"), [Macedonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macedonia_(region) "Macedonia (region)") and [Thrace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrace "Thrace"), roughly on the territories of the [Second Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Bulgarian_Empire "Second Bulgarian Empire"),[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTESan_Stefano,_Berlin_and_Independence-99)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-100) and this day is now [a public holiday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_holidays_in_Bulgaria "Public holidays in Bulgaria") called [National Liberation Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberation_Day_(Bulgaria) "Liberation Day (Bulgaria)").[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-101) The other [Great Powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Powers#History "Great Powers") immediately rejected the treaty out of fear that such a large country in the [Balkans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balkans "Balkans") might threaten their interests. It was superseded by the [Treaty of Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Berlin,_1878 "Treaty of Berlin, 1878"), signed on 13 July. It provided for a much smaller state, the [Principality of Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principality_of_Bulgaria "Principality of Bulgaria"), only comprising Moesia and the region of [Sofia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia "Sofia"), and leaving large populations of ethnic Bulgarians outside the new country.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTESan_Stefano,_Berlin_and_Independence-99)[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-BBCProfile-102) This significantly contributed to Bulgaria's militaristic foreign affairs approach during the first half of the 20th century.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHistorical_Setting-103)

The Bulgarian principality won [a war against Serbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbo-Bulgarian_War "Serbo-Bulgarian War") and incorporated the semi-autonomous Ottoman territory of [Eastern Rumelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Rumelia "Eastern Rumelia") in 1885, proclaiming itself the independent Kingdom of Bulgaria on 5 October 1908.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrampton2007174-104) In the years following independence, Bulgaria increasingly militarised and was often referred to as "the Balkan [Prussia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prussia "Prussia")".[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-105) It became involved in three consecutive conflicts between 1912 and 1918—two [Balkan Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balkan_Wars "Balkan Wars") and [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"). After a disastrous defeat in the [Second Balkan War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Balkan_War "Second Balkan War"), Bulgaria again found itself fighting on the losing side as a result of its alliance with the [Central Powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Powers "Central Powers") in World War I. Despite fielding more than a quarter of its population in a 1,200,000-strong army[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-106)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-107) and achieving several decisive victories at [Doiran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Doiran_(1917) "Battle of Doiran (1917)") and [Monastir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Monastir_(1917) "Battle of Monastir (1917)"), the country capitulated in 1918. The war resulted in significant territorial losses and a total of 87,500 soldiers killed.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-108) More than 253,000 refugees from the lost territories [immigrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immigration "Immigration") to Bulgaria from 1912 to 1929,[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-109) placing additional strain on the already ruined national economy.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-110)

[![Image 23: A portrait of Tsar Boris III](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/BASA-3K-7-342-28-Boris_III_of_Bulgaria.jpeg/250px-BASA-3K-7-342-28-Boris_III_of_Bulgaria.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BASA-3K-7-342-28-Boris_III_of_Bulgaria.jpeg)

Tsar Boris III

The resulting political unrest led to the establishment of a royal [authoritarian dictatorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authoritarianism "Authoritarianism") by Tsar [Boris III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_III_of_Bulgaria "Boris III of Bulgaria") (1918–1943). Bulgaria entered World War II in 1941 as a member of [the Axis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axis_powers "Axis powers") but declined to participate in [Operation Barbarossa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Barbarossa "Operation Barbarossa") and [saved its Jewish population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rescue_of_the_Bulgarian_Jews "Rescue of the Bulgarian Jews") from deportation to [concentration camps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_concentration_camps "Nazi concentration camps").[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBulgaria_in_World_War_II:_The_Passive_Alliance-111) The sudden death of Boris III in mid-1943 pushed the country into political turmoil as the war turned against Germany, and the communist guerrilla movement gained momentum. The government of [Bogdan Filov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bogdan_Filov "Bogdan Filov") subsequently failed to achieve peace with the Allies. Bulgaria did not comply with Soviet demands to expel German forces from its territory, resulting in a declaration of war and an invasion by the USSR in September 1944.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWartime_Crisis-112) The communist-dominated [Fatherland Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatherland_Front_(Bulgaria) "Fatherland Front (Bulgaria)") took power, ended participation in the Axis and joined the Allied side until the war ended.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-113) Bulgaria suffered little war damage and the Soviet Union demanded no reparations. But all wartime territorial gains, with the notable exception of [Southern Dobrudzha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Craiova "Treaty of Craiova"), were lost.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_Soviet_Occupation-114)
